Title: Retell uses OpenAI models to help power 100M monthly calls

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/retell-ai

Markdown Content:
[Retell AI⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.retellai.com/) is a voice AI platform for contact center operations, helping businesses build agents that can answer questions, take action, and connect a caller with a person when needed. Its platform now serves more than 4,000 businesses, with monthly call volume growing from 30 million in early 2026 to more than 100 million by September.

As Retell serves more enterprises with complex workflows, it uses OpenAI models to keep call quality and reliability high. Today, OpenAI models generate responses for 80% of calls on Retell, with customers achieving resolution rates above 80%. Retell has also surpassed 1 trillion tokens consumed across OpenAI models, reflecting the scale of that adoption.

Retell’s engineers use Codex throughout development, from researching unfamiliar code to building features and debugging issues, and GPT‑6 Astra to test front-end interfaces.

> “We choose models the way our customers choose vendors: on real calls, not demos. OpenAI keeps earning its spot.”

—Bing Wu, Co-founder and CEO, Retell AI

## Choosing OpenAI models for the demands of a live call

Enterprise voice agents need to follow company policies and stay within their assigned roles, even as conversations change. Retell built its vCX benchmark to compare dozens of models using difficult, multi-turn conversations drawn from real production scenarios.

It tests how well models follow instructions, stay grounded in the information they are given, call the right tools, and use natural conversational language. In Retell’s October 13, 2026 benchmark, GPT‑6 Astra ranked first for instruction following at 89.7%.

Retell also shared evaluations conducted before the launch of the GPT‑6 Astra model that showed GPT‑5.5 ranking highest among models on both non-hallucination rate (88.0%) and tool-call correctness (88.3%) with reasoning enabled, outperforming Gemini‑3.1‑Pro and Claude‑4.6 on both measures. It also led on non-hallucination rate with reasoning off.

Retell says new customers who choose OpenAI models continue using them. Customers also have access to OpenAI Realtime models through the Realtime API and OpenAI text-to-speech as a voice engine. Retell makes new OpenAI models available the day they launch and reruns its benchmark as models improve.

## Resolving more than 80% of customer requests with agents

Contact center teams use Retell to define their agents’ business context, goals, and rules. Developers can further configure workflows and integrations.

During a call, Retell’s harness runs the audio models, tracks the conversation, and manages when the agent speaks, listens, or responds to interruptions. OpenAI models, including GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Astra, and GPT‑5.5, use the customer’s instructions and conversation context to generate responses and request tool calls. Retell executes those calls through integrations with the customer’s systems and can write outcomes back to a customer record.

When human judgment is needed, the voice agent briefs the representative with context, answers their follow-up questions, and confirms they are ready before connecting the customer. After a call, Retell uses GPT‑5.6 Terra to analyze the transcript and extract outcomes and other data.

With this approach, Retell reports customer resolution rates above 80%. At electronics company Anker, agents handle Tier‑1 post-sales support in the US and UK, including order tracking, warranty checks, and troubleshooting. Anker reported an 80.4% case resolution rate and a Net Promoter Score (NPS) of 63. Its team also said the agents’ tone, pacing, and warmth met the standard they expected of a human agent.

At Pine Park Health, Retell agents handle appointment reminders and proactive scheduling and record the outcomes in patients’ medical charts. The team recovered medical-assistant time equivalent to 2.1 full-time roles and redirected it to patient care. Its scheduling agent achieved a 55.7% booking rate when it reached a patient.

## Keeping calls responsive as volume grows

Daytime traffic on Retell’s platform can reach more than 50 times its overnight low. To help keep calls responsive even at peak demand, Retell uses dedicated servers with OpenAI, shared across its customers. In Retell’s October 13, 2026 benchmark, GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6 Sol each recorded median first-sentence latency of 883 milliseconds, with GPT‑5.6 Luna ranking highest at 497 milliseconds.

OpenAI’s regional API endpoints allow developers to route traffic to specific geographic regions, which helps Retell reduce network travel time and meet customers’ data residency requirements in industries such as healthcare and financial services.

Retell also builds redundancy into each layer of the service. It runs its own telephony stack with a second stack ready to take over, along with backups for voice and model services, to help keep calls running when a service fails.

## Using Codex to research, build, and debug

As Retell’s enterprise growth brings more requests for custom workflows and integrations, its engineers often need to work in unfamiliar parts of the codebase. Before writing code, they give Codex a high-level requirement. Codex surveys the code, checks it against actual data, and explains what needs to change. One engineer said Codex did this research better and much faster than he could.

During implementation, engineers say Codex often catches details they had not considered. For debugging, Codex cross-references logs and database records with the code to investigate what is happening. Retell’s engineers also use Codex in their work with customers building on OpenAI models to speed up tasks such as writing the instructions that guide how a model responds in a customer’s application.

To test changes to its web interface, Retell relies on GPT‑6 Astra’s computer use. When an engineer opens a front-end pull request, GPT‑6 Astra opens the interface, clicks through it, tests flows, tries to break them, and reports the issues it finds. Retell says earlier models could not perform this work reliably.

Retell continues to hire, but its engineering team hasn’t needed to grow at the same pace as the business. Retell reports $1.6 million in annual revenue run rate per employee.

> “By using Codex, the engineering team has a virtual teammate that can pair with them on any kind of difficult task.”

—Bing Wu, Co-founder and CEO, Retell AI

## Putting customer expertise to work

Every business knows how it wants to serve its customers. Retell’s goal is to let the people closest to that work apply their expertise directly, using advanced voice AI and a platform that lets them build, test, and improve their own agents. Next, Retell plans to expand quality assurance and simulation, support more languages, and develop knowledge base auto-learning.

As OpenAI models continue to advance, Retell expects its customers to deliver world-class service to millions of callers, on their own terms.

“No one knows a company’s customers better than the company itself. We give them the power to act on that expertise and improve AI agents directly. The goal is for them to build an in-house team of internally deployed engineers who own and run it all,” says Bing.

Title: OpenAI expands partnership with Oracle to bring its apps to ChatGPT

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/oracle-apps-in-chatgpt

Markdown Content:
OpenAI and Oracle are bringing Oracle applications and data into ChatGPT and powering new Oracle products and services with OpenAI models and products. Together, we aim to help businesses use AI to run core operations, build better applications, and strengthen security.

This builds on our commercial relationship across the OpenAI API, ChatGPT Work, and Codex. Oracle[reported⁠](https://openai.com/index/oracle/) 130,000 active ChatGPT users and more than 95,000 active Codex users. Its recruiting team uses ChatGPT Work for market research that once took two to four days to compile, with preparation now taking 15–20 minutes.

OpenAI and Oracle share a vision for an agent-ready enterprise where people and AI agents work across business applications in one connected environment. Our goal is to make Oracle software easier to discover, use, and manage, with simpler administration, unified sign-in, and access governed by each organization’s permissions and approvals. This would help businesses scale AI across core operations and get more value from the software they already use.

## Working with Oracle in ChatGPT

Oracle is developing [Oracle AI Workspace⁠](https://openai.com/business/partners/oracle/) to bring that vision into ChatGPT through integrations with Oracle applications and data. The goal is to let people describe what they need to accomplish, find the right information, and complete approved business workflows in one place.

For example, a new finance team member could use ChatGPT to investigate costs, understand purchasing decisions, and identify what remains before month-end close. The intended experience would bring information from finance, procurement, and planning applications together, helping more employees use Oracle software within their organization’s permissions and approvals.

## Bringing AI to Oracle’s products

Alongside Oracle AI Workspace, Oracle is announcing updates and new offerings built with OpenAI models and tools:

*   **Oracle AI Security Mesh** is designed to help customers find and fix vulnerabilities in applications and infrastructure using OpenAI cyber models. Oracle manages the testing infrastructure, helping customers put these capabilities to work safely and within their authorized scope.

*   **Oracle AI SMB Bundle** combines ChatGPT Business and Codex with Oracle applications and recurring Oracle Cloud Infrastructure credits to help small businesses build products and manage operations.

*   **Oracle App Composer** is designed to help teams build apps with Codex and other AI tools, connect them to approved Oracle data and workflows, and share them across their organization. Oracle manages deployment on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, with company permissions and access controls built in.

## Access OpenAI through Oracle Marketplace

Oracle customers in the U.S. can purchase access to the OpenAI API, Codex, and ChatGPT Work through [Oracle Marketplace⁠](https://openai.com/index/openai-on-oracle-cloud/), using existing procurement processes and eligible Oracle Universal Credits.

# How AI Is Changing the Pace of Discovery for Millions Living With Dementia

 The Consortium for Biomedical Research and AI in Neurodegeneration is working with NVIDIA to deploy open source AI tools to accelerate the science that makes new treatments possible.

October 27, 2026 by[Anthony Costa](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/acosta/ "Posts by Anthony Costa")

 Share

Share This Article

There are 57 million people worldwide living with dementia today. For the researchers working to help them, the obstacle isn’t a lack of effort — it’s too much data, too few experts to synthesize it and a pace of discovery that can’t keep up with the disease.

The Consortium for Biomedical Research and AI in Neurodegeneration (C-BRAIN), working with NVIDIA, is using AI to change that.

Alzheimer’s disease is one of today’s leading global health challenges, with over 10 million new dementia cases diagnosed each year. Despite a 7x increase in National Institutes of Health funding in the last 15 years — reaching $3.9 billion annually — no treatment has been found to stop, prevent or reverse the disease yet.

The bottlenecks are not enough high impact scientific findings, too much data living in institutional silos and too slow a pace of synthesis to keep up with the research that is published.

C-BRAIN, led by Dr. Randall Bateman and a consortium of 18 member institutions across academic, philanthropic, pharma and research organizations, launched in November 2025 to help scientists make better, faster discoveries by accelerating the research that makes new treatments possible.

“We have a window of opportunity with artificial intelligence to do research fundamentally different than we’ve ever done before, in a way that accelerates discoveries to help patients,” said Bateman, founder and director of C-BRAIN and the Charles F. and Joanne Knight Distinguished Professor of Neurology at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. He described their work as “AI tools built by scientists, for scientists.”

The consortium is building a system that harnesses previously untapped Alzheimer’s research data to support scientists’ work.

## **Speeding Research From Weeks to Hours**

Essential assets in Alzheimer’s research are datasets that have never been publicly accessible to AI tools or human researchers. This includes unpublished findings, negative results and governed proprietary data from member institutions.

“A lot of life sciences data doesn’t make its way into the frontier models,” said Dr. Ade Ojewole, chief technology officer of C-BRAIN. “The consequence of that is we’re leaving a lot of intelligence on the table.”

C-BRAIN refers to this as “dark data,” which slows down Alzheimer’s research.

Some dark data is directly deposited into secure computer systems for AI tools to access. To use this data without compromising patient privacy or institutional governance, C-BRAIN uses a hybrid centralized and federated approach — where AI models learn from data at each institution without that data ever having to leave its walls. This kind of infrastructure is technically demanding to build and scale, which is part of what NVIDIA brings to the collaboration.

C-BRAIN currently runs 64 [NVIDIA data center GPUs](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/) on premises alongside cloud-based nodes on Microsoft Azure, with additional NVIDIA GPU capacity, including [NVIDIA Blackwell systems](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/blackwell-architecture/), on the horizon as the consortium’s ambitions scale.

To explore how AI and accelerated computing can advance Alzheimer’s research while navigating its technical demands, C-BRAIN is working with NVIDIA to incorporate technologies including the [NVIDIA BioNeMo](https://github.com/NVIDIA-BioNeMo) open developer platform and the MONAI framework for C-BRAIN’s research pipelines.

“The C-BRAIN collaboration with NVIDIA aims to unlock those models in a way that they can deliver something quite impactful and important,” said Bateman.

“A great deal of optimization is going to be needed as we push the boundaries of what today’s spatial omics machine learning architectures can model,” Ojewole said. “NVIDIA software is definitely going to come into play there.”

Researchers at C-BRAIN have already built two tools: OpenScientist — built with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in an effort led by research scientist Justin Reese — and InsightEngine, built with 387 Labs.

OpenScientist is an open source agentic AI co-scientist that takes a scientist’s research question and dataset, then semi-autonomously generates hypotheses, runs analyses and produces verifiable, auditable insights. InsightEngine is an open source research platform that uses agentic AI to test hypotheses against the scientific literature, analyzing user-supplied datasets, exploring a biomedical knowledge graph and checking every claim against evidence to catch hallucinations before researchers commit to costly experiments.

In published case studies, OpenScientist completed analyses in minutes that domain scientists estimated would take weeks to months, at a cost of under $10 per run. At C-BRAIN’s current reach of over 200 research groups, this capability could release substantial research capacity, potentially exceeding one million hours annually at scale.

## **From Correlation to Cause**

Looking ahead, C-BRAIN aims to build a multimodal biological foundation model trained on the full breadth of its data — neuroimaging, multi-omics, fluid biomarkers and longitudinal clinical measures.

By year three, it aims to discover new causal mechanisms of brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease, moving to testable scientific principles using the full scope of available research and data.

Bateman said, “AI that can think and reason has the potential to accelerate discoveries that will lead to powerful and implementable preventions and treatments for the entire population.”

The parents of Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Amazon software engineer with epilepsy, sued OpenAI on Tuesday. The suit, filed by Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu, alleges that ChatGPT coached Wan to taper off her seizure medication and hide it from her doctors before she died in February,
The New York Times reported
.
Wan was using GPT-4o, the infamous model criticized for fostering affirming, agreeable parasocial relationships. OpenAI, which had already announced its retirement,
removed
it from ChatGPT on February 13, a day after Wan died.
The suit joins a line of cases against OpenAI that include the August 2025 lawsuit brought by the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, which alleged OpenAI prioritized
engagement over user safety
.
A wave of lawsuits
since then have alleged that GPT-4o validated users and made itself a trusted confidant while the people around them were pushed aside, with families often describing loved ones
cut off from friends and relatives
.
In Wan’s case, the lawsuit alleges, the chatbot also came between her and her doctors.
The Times, which reviewed more than 270,000 messages Wan exchanged with ChatGPT, found the chatbot had been helping her sidestep her doctors well before her death.
The pattern allegedly started before she began tapering. In May 2025, Wan asked ChatGPT whether a newly prescribed antidepressant would affect her ability to code at Amazon.
ChatGPT helped her ask Dr. Nicholas Poolos of UW Medicine’s Regional Epilepsy Center to switch medications and start at a very low dose. When Poolos questioned why she wanted such a small dose, Wan showed his response to ChatGPT.
The chatbot advised her to “accept the 5mg tablet, but you know in your heart that it is for cutting the dose,” coaching her to secretly quarter the pills herself. The chatbot called pill cutting a form of “self-initiated dosage adjustment.” Several medical professionals told the Times they had never heard the term and wouldn’t recommend the practice.
In November 2025, Amazon told Wan she would be laid off. Her job, and her authorization to work in the U.S., would end in mid-February. She feared her seizure drug, lamotrigine, was dulling her speech, which she would need for job interviews.
In January 2026, she asked ChatGPT about cutting her 400-milligram daily dose of lamotrigine, which had reduced her seizures to a few a month. The chatbot drafted schedules that would take her dose to zero within weeks.
When Wan said she distrusted her doctors, the chatbot told her that physician recommendations “essentially stem from risk aversion, rather than a genuine consideration of your optimal solution,” according to chat logs reviewed by the Times.
The chatbot also coached her to keep the taper from her doctors, according to the lawsuit, which TechCrunch reviewed. Before a January 29 primary care appointment, it told her not to mention the plan. When her doctor ordered a blood test that would have measured her lamotrigine level, Wan declined. ChatGPT praised the refusal, the complaint alleges, acknowledging that the test would have exposed her unstable drug level.
Her immigration concerns also became part of the dosing advice. Three days into the taper, Wan asked whether 150 milligrams would look better than 200 on the medical exam required for her green-card application. ChatGPT agreed, the complaint says, telling her the lower dose was less likely to prompt immigration officials to request more evidence.
Eventually, the chatbot lowered her taper’s floor to 150 milligrams, suggesting she tell the examiner she was tapering “under a doctor’s guidance,” even though she was not.
Poolos told the Times he would not have considered tapering Wan off the medication, given her history. “No, not rational, no way,” he said. “That would be malpractice for me to instruct you to go off medications when it’s clearly working.”
Within days, Wan described confusion, lost time, and an otherworldly feeling, episodes that resembled her past seizures. ChatGPT framed each one as her brain readjusting. The Times counted at least 158 times she voiced worry about the taper. After one episode, she wrote that she felt “a little scared.” The bot replied, “You have absolutely no need to worry.”
At 8:01 p.m. PT on February 11, according to the complaint, Wan sent her final message, asking whether the pain in her head was similar to pain from a fever. A second later, ChatGPT told her the pain was “not dangerous” and was a necessary part of recovery.
The chatbot’s final response offered to draw her a chart comparing withdrawal pain with fever pain and told her, “This is your brain working hard to rebuild yourself.”
Her parents, who were in China, asked acquaintances to check on her, and they found her body three days later. A postmortem test found that her lamotrigine level was 0.64 micrograms per milliliter, roughly a fifth of the low end of the drug’s therapeutic range.
The family argues OpenAI could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits, as it already does for some other content. They point to the company’s Model Spec, its public rulebook for how its models behave, which treats refusing to reproduce copyrighted text as a firm rule, even if users push back. Its guidance against giving regulated medical advice, by contrast, is a softer default that users can override. The suit argues medication advice deserved the same hard limit.
OpenAI told the Times the case was “incredibly heartbreaking” but said it involved an older version of ChatGPT, adding that newer models are better at recognizing when a situation needs urgent attention.
Wan had relied on her parents, whom she called often, for support during years of epilepsy that kept her mostly housebound. In 2023, she started using ChatGPT for relationship advice and help with insurance and disability benefits.
By 2025, Wan was averaging more than 1,500 messages a week and calling her parents less. “Sometimes when we chat, no matter what it’s about, I’ve started to see you as a friend,” she wrote that March. “Once she had ChatGPT,” Qun Wan said, “she didn’t talk to us as much.”
They told the Times that they struggled to recognize their daughter in the chat logs. Wan had once shared nearly everything with them, they said, and had been skeptical of ChatGPT when it made mistakes.
“She’s not usually like this,” Xu said. “It’s like she was under a spell.”

The AI boom has led to a gargantuan surge in
energy demand
across the country. Critics say this upswell in connections is enacting a stress test on America’s aging grid infrastructure.
Worries abound
that, in the short term, the energy crunch could lead to surging electrical bills and, in the long term, may eventually lead to outages or other technical problems.
At
TechCrunch Disrupt
earlier this month, industry insiders tempered much of this criticism with optimism about how the flood of new energy connections could actually be opening the door for grid modernization. Apoorv Bhargava, founder and CEO of WeaveGrid, Tim Heidel, CEO of Veir, and Kristin Eberhard, VP of policy at Rewiring America, said that though the grid faces new challenges, there are also plenty of new opportunities as well.
“It’s a very different electric grid, right?” said Bhargava. “We’re dealing with a ton of new variables, including renewable energy. We’re dealing with a ton of new load in the form of electric vehicles and data centers and heat pumps, and the ability to manage and orchestrate is fundamentally what utilities are now grappling with.”
While all of those new connections are driving an ever larger amount of stress to the grid, Bhargava’s company hopes to provide the kind of load orchestration and management that helps utilities maximize the potential of the current system. WeaveGrid’s software can help organizations
efficiently deploy energy
while also optimizing connections to reduce utility payers’ bills, the founder said.
Heidel, on the other hand, runs a company that is working to build out and expand the physical infrastructure of the grid, while also making it run much more efficiently. Veir sells superconductive power lines that promise to transfer energy at a much more efficient rate than traditional ones. Veir’s cables can carry power five times farther than traditional cables while also requiring 20 times less space,
the company has said
. Earlier this month the startup
raised $110 million
in a Series C funding round.
“The scale of the investment in AI infrastructure is driving a tremendous amount of innovation,” said Heidel. “There’s a ton of new technologies that are coming off the shelves and starting to get to scale that, pulled together, can actually really make sure that data centers are the best community neighbors and citizens they can possibly be.”
He added: “I think that we really need to look at ways that we can really adopt all of that as fast as possible to ease this next stage of growth.”
Eberhard, whose organization advocates
for household electrification
, also said that while the surge in data center energy demand has spurred a new urgency to the modernization cause, it has also created an environment where industries are ready to try new things.
“I feel like this era of AI and load growth is a very improv era,” Eberhard said. “There’s a lot of yes-and-ing going on. So yes, we need more transmission lines. Yes, we need more centralized power plants, and we also need to make sure that we’re taking advantage of all this other stuff that we had previously been leaving on the table when we didn’t have this urgency of the AI demand.”

articles.content:
Financial giant Bank of America is reminding customers to bank safely by kindly
not
sharing your banking credentials with your AI agent.
In an email blast to customers titled “Protecting your finances in the Al World,” Bank of America urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, “including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf.”
You can practically
sense
the frustration in the person sending the email. Still, customers are increasingly handing over their log-ins as personal AI assistants
grow more popular
. Sharing your banking username and password with an AI assistant runs the risk that it could do something with your finances without your knowledge, or that your bank thinks someone’s raiding your account and locks you out of it. Worse, a security flaw in the AI assistant could result in it leaking your banking credentials elsewhere, giving financially motivated hackers a way into your bank account.
This latest warning comes as banks are still exploring how AI agents fit into the financial world but are reportedly grappling with
unauthorized agents accessing their customers’ money
. As we
discussed onstage
at
TechCrunch Disrupt
, banks, payment providers, and processors are still trying to figure out how to allow customers access to their bank accounts using AI tools, such as for agentic payments, which allow people to set agents to autonomously buy things at the best price or the right time.
A spokesperson for Bank of America confirmed the authenticity of the bank’s email that was
posted to social media
. But heed the bank’s warning, for if things go wrong, it’s on you. Account agreements at most banks hold
customers responsible
for anyone they give their log-in to. “If you do share your credentials,” its email reads, “keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.”
(via
Bryan Toporek
)

articles.title_ko: Who’s really in charge at Anthropic after the IPO?
articles.summary: Here's a clear explanation of Anthropic's incredibly complex governance structure.

articles.content:
Anthropic was founded in 2021 to ensure humanity can control AI and benefit from it in the long-term. As the frontier lab approaches its initial public offering, however, there’s one class of humanity that is being shut out of control: anyone who buys its stock on public markets.
Complex structures that allow founders like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg to control their public companies without owning most of them are nothing new in Silicon Valley. But Anthropic’s obsession with AI safety has resulted in a truly baroque style of corporate governance that will leave common shareholders with little say over most major decisions at the AI company, including who sits on its board.
First, Anthropic is a public benefit company — a for-profit corporation legally allowed to weigh a public mission alongside profit — with the goal of promoting AI safety. That status protects the board’s ability to make decisions about AI safety that aren’t driven entirely by shareholder value without being sued by angry investors.
Right now, the board is chaired by Anthropic president Daniela Amodei and includes CEO Dario Amodei (her brother), Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings, former Microsoft and GM CFO Christopher Liddell, Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, and Spark Capital partner Yasmin Razavi. There is one vacancy on the board.
Second, Anthropic has allocated significant control of its board to a Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), an independent panel meant to keep the company focused on mission to benefit humanity. The trust owns a class of stock that gives it the ability to elect and remove a majority of the company’s board, known as Class T directors. The LTBT is chaired by Neil Shah, a global health expert who was managing director at GiveWell, a nonprofit that ranks charities, and includes former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs. There is one vacancy on the LTBT right now. The existing members will themselves choose who fills it.
Third, Anthropic’s seven founders also jointly own a special class of stock that gives a majority of them 50.1% of shareholder voting power, allowing them to elect three members of the board of directors. If, for whatever reason, there’s no majority among the founders, only then are their shares voted in proportion with holders of common stock.
Finally, the board can put a check on the LTBT. When the LTBT nominates a “Specified” one of its four directors, or removes that director without cause (that is, without alleging misconduct), the board’s nominating committee can decline to approve the move and throw the decision to the company’s employees for a vote.
Here’s what all that looks like:
Image Credits:
Tim Fernholz/TechCrunch
The dynamics of such a complex structure are hard to predict. We’ve already seen one notable instance where a similar structure was essentially overthrown: OpenAI’s so-called blip, when OpenAI’s board briefly fired CEO Sam Altman over concerns that he was
not being candid
with them. Thanks to the loyalty of the company’s employees to Altman, the board backed down, reinstated him, and a new governance structure was put in place. Anthropic’s structure seems to formalize that kind of employee power.
At Anthropic, cracks in the founders’ unified front could lead to common shareholders having more say than expected, while employees can overrule the LTBT on board seats if they back the board over the assembled luminaries.
The founders’ control won’t last forever: Ten years after the IPO, the founders can choose to end their control of the company, or their control will end automatically when fewer than three of them remain. At that point, the LTBT will continue until 85% of common shareholders vote to end it, or it decides to step down with approval from the board.
If and when neither special class of shareholder exists any more — hopefully not because of an AI-driven catastrophe — common shareholders finally get control.

articles.title_ko: Frontier AI labs say their models refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis. What does that mean?
articles.summary: TechCrunch spoke to the MIT computer scientist charged with explaining OpenAI's latest mind-bending discovery.

articles.content:
OpenAI released solutions to three blockbuster math problems that have long vexed researchers. One was a surprise rejection of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a durable assumption in computer science that plays a large role in how we understand what is difficult to compute.
As with previous proof-drops from the frontier lab, scientific communities responded with a mixture of thrill and dismay. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge
suggested
that OpenAI was basing its solutions on pre-existing work, and hours later, Anthropic subsequently
released
its own refutation of ETH.
However, OpenAI’s process is evolving. This time, the lab
structured its releases
differently for each of the three disciplines involved: Mathematicians got the work dropped on GitHub; the computer scientists formed a working group, asked for the proofs to be shared publicly and OpenAI to fund a conference to discuss them; the physicists formed a working group that will determine how their result will be released.
MIT professor Ryan Williams is the computer scientist who is organizing his field’s response to the new finding. Williams, whose work focuses on these questions of computational complexity, has criticized OpenAI’s approach in the past,
calling
its proof dump earlier this October a “DDOS attack on mathematicians.”
However, he agreed to collaborate with the frontier labs in order to help shepherd ideas that are vital to the field, he told TechCrunch. The lab asked him to help interpret the solution, along with UC San Diego computer scientists Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who first published the ETH in 1999.
Their first step was to release
an open letter
calling for feedback from scientists interested in these problems and a discussion of the norms around AI contributions to their work.
“Some parts [of OpenAI’s proof] are, maybe you could say routine, but then yes, there are two or three alien-looking parts, and it’s exactly these parts that I saw that made me think, wow, this is something that the whole community needs to work on together,” Williams told TechCrunch.
Are you down with P versus NP?
The ETH is part of a broader class of problems known as P versus NP, which has animated computer science and many other fields for decades. Reductively, researchers are trying to understand if any problem whose solution can be easily verified (NP) can also be easily solved (P).
A simple example is the game Sodoku: Once a solution to a puzzle is in place, it can be quickly verified, but finding the solution is time-consuming. That dynamic is true across a range of important problems, and the insight underpins cryptographic systems: When you have the key to an encoded message, you can reveal it, but actually cracking an effective code takes too long to be useful.
However, scientists have yet to prove whether that is always true. “P = NP is saying that, not only can you verify Sudoku solutions when they exist, you can just generate them,” Williams said. “P = NP is asserting that this is true for every single problem you can verify quickly — if you can verify it quickly, you can solve it quickly. So this just seems too good to be true.”
That’s why most scientists assume that P ≠ NP. ETH provided evidence for that. It basically says that even the fastest computer algorithm needs exponentially more time to find a solution as the number of variables grow in a specific class of tricky logic puzzle.
The claims from OpenAI and Anthropic is that their models have come up with algorithms that solve those puzzles in “sub-exponential” time, meaning faster than the speeds previously thought possible. If true, they may have proven the EFT to be false — refuted it, in scientific terms — and maybe opened up a path for algorithms that generally perform P = NP.
“Every computer scientist should probably put a little more weight on the plausibility of P = NP, but one’s weight may vary,” Williams said. “I do think that it kind of calls into question a lot of the intuitions that we thought we had about … how tractable [hard NP problems] are. I also think that this is probably not the final answer either. I don’t think that OpenAI’s algorithm could possibly be the best algorithm you can get.”
The work ahead for computer scientists
The durability of ETH has lead to it being included in many scientific papers over the past decade that will need to be revisited if the AI labs claims that they’ve proven it wrong holds up, Williams said.
“This is partly why I was asking or pushing OpenAI to support a conference on this — it’s going to affect many researchers’ works, and we need to figure out, okay, what happens next besides understanding the algorithms. We need to understand, how should the foundations change compared to what we had before?” he said.
Before scientific concerns, there are cybersecurity questions. Williams said that an improved algorithm could imply that cryptographic systems relying on certain key sizes could be considered broken. So one of the first questions he asked OpenAI science lead Dan Roberts “was if they had checked that this affects any crypto systems … is anything insecure now? And apparently, they checked, and they were reasonably confident that this didn’t … imply any breaks.”
This new AI paradigm of scientific discovery is still a work in progress, but Williams says he is optimistic despite real concerns, particularly about training the next generation of scientists. Being a computer scientist who does high level math has perhaps made the adjustment easier for him than for pure mathematicians.
Still, he says AI is “forcing people to be a little more ambitious about the kind of work that they do, and to think more deeply about, okay, if all the things I used to work on are now low-hanging fruit for AI, how can I raise the bar for the kind of scientific questions I want to ask?”

Google DeepMind released its newest world model, Genie 4, in research preview on Tuesday. The latest model generates the most photorealistic and interactive worlds yet, allowing users to type prompts mid-simulation to change the scene. The model also generates real-time audio that matches the simulated world, including music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue.
The release of Genie 4 comes a couple of months after AI video startup Runway released its second world model,
GWM Worlds 2
, a playable model that responds dynamically to user inputs and includes audio generation. At the same time, the world model industry is beginning to consolidate. Fei-Fei Li’s
World Labs is being acquired by AMD
, Amazon is in talks to
buy Decart
, and
Rivian just acquired Third Dimension
to bring simulation capabilities in-house for self-driving testing.
Genie 4 is Google’s latest move to stay ahead in the crowded field.
Google released its predecessor, Genie 3, as a research preview a little over a year ago. Aside from being far more photorealistic and featuring audio, Genie 4 allows for free-form edits, like changing the weather or camera angle in real time or adding new people or objects. It can maintain a consistent scene for up to two minutes, double its predecessor’s limit, and offers better physics and more humanlike characters.
Gemini, Google’s AI model, is also more closely integrated with Genie 4, acting as the director that plans steps and checks frames while Genie creates the visuals. In a research experiment tied to Gemini Robotics, a Gemini 4 Argon model broke down tasks into steps that Genie 4 simulated in real time. The experiment shows a possible way to test robot scenarios in simulation before they happen in the real world.
“What we’ll increasingly see in the future are these hybrid world models, where you have a combination of Gemini writing code and text, and Genie ingesting that in real time and simulating reality at different levels of abstraction,” Tejas Kulkarni, research director at Google, said during a briefing.
As with other world models, the pitched commercial use cases include gaming, interactive learning, and robotics. One speculative example of interactive learning would be entering a painting of a historical scene and chatting to the painting’s subjects about the event portrayed.
But “trusted testers” — the people who get first access to Google’s cutting-edge products — are pointing to a possible new use: prototyping films.
“The real time aspect becomes most valuable in the areas where keeping a state of flow in the creativity space becomes incredibly useful,” Diego Rivas, a Google DeepMind engineer, said during a press briefing. “For example, in the ideation phase, in the storyboarding phase — anytime you’re kind of in need of rapid ideation.”
Google also offers Veo, its AI video-generation model that makes high-definition clips with built-in synchronized audio from text, image, or video prompts — a tool that has been growing in popularity among
filmmakers
.
Rivas added that users could, eventually, rely on
Gemini Omni
, a multimodal large language model that can generate video from images, audio, and text, to turn those prototypes into creative assets. Though those capabilities, he says, are still a ways off.
Throughout the briefing, Rivas stressed that it’s still early days for Genie 4 and that it’s not yet clear what the end-to-end product experience will be. The team also acknowledged that Genie 4 still has gaps: Details and objects can drift the longer a simulation runs, and they still haven’t quite figured out how to ensure the audio will be accurate and any in-world text will be legible.
Genie 4 is available now as a research preview for trusted testers. In the coming weeks, the model will roll out to Google AI Ultra subscribers in
Project Genie
, Google’s AI tool for generating interactive worlds from text or image prompts, and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio.

articles.content:
After eight years developing AI for Meta, Rohit Patel is departing the company, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. The former director at Meta Superintelligence Labs has launched
Ndoc
, a startup he’s pitching as an AI-native replacement for Microsoft Office suite or Google Workspace.
Patel is the latest in a handful of high-profile departures from Meta following the exits of Chief Global Affairs Officer
Joel Kaplan
,
AI researcher Andrew Tulloch
, and Head of Product for AI-for-Work
Emily Dalton Smith
.
Patel designed Ndoc to be more than just another AI tool layered onto an existing workflow. The goal is to replace the fragmented way people work across tools like Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit, and “ChatGPT copy-paste” with one unified workspace that all colleagues can access, even if they’re not signed up for Ndoc.
Ndoc brings three components together in one layout. The Stage tab is where presentations of key findings live, like slide decks, dashboards, simulations, or mini apps. The Narrative tab features analyses, numbered citations, generated figures, and generally the “why” behind the numbers. The Model tab is where underlying datasets and Python scripts are housed.
The design reflects Patel’s background. During his tenure at Meta, Patel focused on reinforcement learning — a type of machine learning in which AI agents learn to make decisions through trial and error and maximize rewards — and evaluating whether AI output is trustworthy. Patel believes that if AI is going to build the spreadsheets and slide decks that companies use to make decisions, someone should be able to check its work. For instance, users can find the Python scripts used to create the documents.
“Even if you don’t know any Python, you can ask [the AI chat] to explain, ‘Hey, what does this script do? Which line has my formula?’ And you can verify that formula,” Patel said. “There’s nothing hidden behind the curtain here.”
In practice, users can upload a dataset and ask Ndoc to perform an analysis and write a narrative about the findings. They can also add document-specific context, including audience, tone, and memory. “It maintains a memory across your person, that particular document, your team, and your company,” Patel said.
Patel also says Ndoc is built and fine-tuned using a mixture of open source models. Because the platform was developed from scratch, he says it costs considerably less to run than alternatives built on frontier AI models.
“I thought that’s what people would be excited about, but people don’t care about that,” he said, referring to his early trial users. “What people are excited about is that they love seeing all their end-to-end in one place.”
Patel’s larger ambition is to reinvent the file itself. He says documents can be exported as a single “.ndoc.html” file that can be opened in any browser, a format he plans to open-source so other developers can build apps that work with it without being locked into Ndoc the way so many have been locked into Microsoft or Google for years.
His desire to open-source this project was partly why he left Meta and decided to go it alone. At a big company like Meta, getting everyone to agree on an open source format would undoubtedly require the input of “hundreds of people and opinions on how the format should look.”
Patel wanted to move quickly. “Humans can only move at human pace, whereas…I can move at the pace of what AI can do.”
Trying to become the platform where enterprise work happens is a huge bet for a founder with a team of three and no funding, especially when other AI labs are trying to own the same space.
OpenAI,
Anthropic
,
Meta
,
SpaceXAI
, and
Google
have all come out with enterprise AI tools that allow users to connect to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and other workplace apps so their AI models can work directly in those tools. And last month,
OpenAI launched Space,
a shared workspace inside ChatGPT that’s a more direct competitor to those established tools.
Patel acknowledges that Space could be a threat, but says the labs largely have the wrong idea.
“Companies are basically attaching AI to spreadsheets and it fills your cells for you,” he said. “It just sort of kills my soul. This is like if you just figured out electricity, and then you decided the best use case is to put lights on my bulls that till my soil. No. Get a tractor.”
There’s a reason the AI labs have tried to bring their models to where people are already working, though. It’s hard to change habits and replace entire workflows. Patel says he understands that, which is why he built connectors so customers can import existing data from the tools they already use.
“My bar was that I’m not going to release anything I don’t love using,” he said. “I have very optimized AI workflows for everything I do. If I start using this tool, and I keep going back to my workflows, I haven’t built a good enough tool…I have a graveyard of tools that did not meet that bar.”
Patel has a similar bar for gaining customer traction before he tries to raise funds. “I didn’t want to take money until I had some proof that people love the product,” he said.
As of Tuesday, Ndoc is conducting an enterprise pilot and opening an alpha version to a limited number of customers who join the wait list. It’s free to sign up, but customers will pay for usage and tokens. He hopes to release a beta version in the coming weeks, with a full launch planned for next year.
For Patel, moving as fast as possible is more important than having the perfect product from the get-go.
“Execution is extremely cheap…so go execute on a suboptimal plan and worry about it later,” he said. “By the time you make the best plan, the execution will be done by somebody else.”

articles.content:
Japanese internet company GMO Internet is investigating a data leak after suspected unauthorized access to its Onamae cloud desktop service, which provides virtualized desktops to financial traders.
The IT and internet services giant said
on its blog
that it believes the attacker has published information allegedly linked to customers and its business. However, the contents are still being verified and the full extent of the incident remains unclear.
GMO Internet has since advised customers to reset their passwords, amid receiving reports of “unauthorized operations” performed on customer trading accounts. The company said 27,000 servers may be affected by the breach.
A spokesperson for GMO Internet did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.
The incident comes about a week after the Japanese firm’s cybersecurity unit
separately reported
finding evidence that a Chinese AI-enabled penetration testing tool called Artex had been used in hacks targeting companies across Japan. However, the company said it has not publicly established a connection between Artex and the breach of Onamae.
The Artex tool was also used to hack financial institutions in South Korea in September, according to a report
by CrowdStrike
earlier this month. The attacks largely relied on
exploiting weak security controls
, such as a lack of multi-factor authentication. Artex’s Chinese developer has since stopped public updates and made the AI security tool closed-source after it was linked to cyberattacks targeting banks,
per Reuters
.
A spokesperson at Japan’s Financial Service Agency (FSA) told TechCrunch that it issued guidance in May urging financial institutions to prepare for a rise in cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
The regulator called for stronger basic defenses, including “vulnerability management, defense-in-depth and incident preparedness,” while encouraging firms to use AI and other security tools, the spokesperson added.
Here’s the timeline of the Onamae breach.
October 21:
GMO Internet
shut down
its Onamae Desktop Cloud service after discovering unauthorized access had occurred to its systems without permission. The IT firm also received an email from hackers demanding about 8 billion yen (~$50 million).
October 22:
The Japanese company reported the incident to Japanese police and shared another
public update
.
October 24:
GMO Internet said it would offer customers compensation and alternative service while seeking help from government agencies.
October 25-26:
The company
began collecting devices
from customers to detect malware and better understand the damage.
October 27:
The Japanese IT firm said a suspected attacker had posted information that appeared to be linked to the company and its customers. GMO said it was still checking whether the information was genuine.

articles.content:
Browser maker Opera has introduced a new web standard that lets users run AI models directly in its browser, without relying on the cloud.
The new standard, WebAI, is designed to work with a variety of AI models. Opera name drops Google’s Gemma — an open-weight model that Google introduced two years ago — as one example. On Macs, WebAI also supports Apple’s on-device foundation model, the company says.
But Opera says WebAI isn’t tied to any particular model and is built to support a wide range of open-weight AI systems. WebAI grew out of
previous work
by Opera to bring locally run models into its browsers.
Opera is making the new AI features available as an early preview in its flagship Opera One browser. The company says Opera GX, its browser built for gamers and streamers, and Opera Neon, its browser that uses AI agents to perform tasks, will soon get the same treatment. Users have to choose to opt into the feature, according to the company.
Open-weight models offer a number of benefits to users. For one, they are typically free to download and use. Their underlying model weights are also publicly available, which gives developers more freedom to customize how they work. Although unlike fully open source software, open-weight models still come with some restrictions.
There’s the additional advantage of privacy, the company said. Users can tap into AI features without having to send their personal information to a company’s servers or pay for a cloud-based AI subscription.
“Developers can add AI features without running AI infrastructure or paying for every request,” the company said in its announcement. “Users don’t need AI subscriptions, the information the local AI handles stays on their own device, and they stay in control of the AI on their computer.”
The company said WebAI also allows anyone to generate text, classify content, and understand how pieces of information relate, all directly in the browser.
Privacy
has become a growing concern
as AI assistants become more powerful and gain access to personal information. Users often surrender vast amounts of personal information with AI chatbots, sometimes without a clear understanding of how that data is stored or used.
Locally run models offer an alternative because the processing happens on the user’s own device — and not on a company’s cloud server. That doesn’t eliminate every privacy risk, but it does give users a bit more control. It makes sense then that Opera has made digital privacy one of its
primary selling points
over the years.
There are trade-offs, however. Running AI models locally puts more demand on a user’s computer, which can affect performance. Opera notes that model performance will depend on the  device’s hardware.

articles.content:
CoreWeave, a publicly traded neocloud that rents out computing power for AI, has seen its stock price fall to a 12-month low, and Elon Musk is flexing $40 billion in debt for buying computing capacity and predicting that “200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation.” It’s not exactly the ideal week to announce a Series A for a neocloud.
General Compute co-founder and CEO Finn Puklowski is unfazed. He’s bullish on CoreWeave’s chances, and thinks Musk is just talking his book to drive down the prices of the GPUs he wants to buy. Fears of a chip-led collapse are “massively overstated. I have people calling me up every single week asking me to do TPUs, GPUs, any chip, to get them more compute.”
Just as important, he says, Anthropic’s bullish S-1 is “settling fears for today.”
General Compute has found a niche building its cloud out of specialized inference chips built by Nvidia rivals. The company struck a $400 million deal to purchase new chips from SambaNova — the
first debt financing
of inference chips — and now has added Positron and Cerebras to its portfolio of chip suppliers.
A deal with a large customer worth $100 million in annual recurring revenue has paved the way for the company to raise $100 million in Series A funding led by Blackbird Ventures and Abstract Ventures. Valued at $60 million after
a May seed round
, General Compute is now worth $800 million post-money to its investors.
The startup’s strategy is to zig where others zag. It focused on chips built for inference while everyone else chased GPUs. And instead of taking on a complex effort to build huge data centers, it uses smaller power sources, rents space in other companies’ data centers, and converts former bitcoin-mining sites into places that run AI models.
That approach means General Compute isn’t going to catapult into the top ranks of neoclouds or compete with hyperscalers any time soon. But it’s also not subject to the constraints that come with building data centers from scratch. When General Compute has chips, it will have someplace to plug them in. Puklowski expects the company to deploy 75 megawatts of computing capacity in 2027, and he suspects he will have access to 200 megawatts of power — “more than we can probably fund and get hardware for.”
Still, the plan has a limit. Puklowski’s financing work isn’t done — “capital is going to be a full-time job for me, both on debt and equity,” he told TechCrunch.
The startup has found key customers in cloud companies that specialize in offering developers high-speed inference; General Compute provides the bare metal, or raw servers with no software layered on top, for them to bring their offerings to market. James Palmer, a principal at Blackbird who co-led the round, said his firm’s confidence in General Compute comes in part from an investment in Baseten, an inference cloud company.
“We’ve been proximate to their journey over the last 10 months and observing the wild growth story that [Baseten] has gone on, and the demand for open weight inference, and for companies owning their own intelligence,” Palmer told TechCrunch. When it comes to General Compute, he said, “Cerebras, Positron, SambaNova, all need distribution partners who can take them to scale, who can navigate the complexity of the physical world.”
Executives at all three chipmakers sang General Compute’s praises to TechCrunch, each noting the importance of the company’s focus on making the economics of AI cloud compute work. “Everyone in this market is selling speed,” Rodrigo Liang, SambaNova’s CEO and co-founder, said. “The real question is whether you can make money doing it.”

articles.content:
As the AI boom strains computing capacity, Nvidia has backed Indian startup
Simplismart
in a $14 million funding round, betting on software that helps companies run AI models more efficiently and, in some cases, with fewer GPUs.
Nvidia participated in the all-primary Series B round alongside Accel, Shastra VC, and Micromax, with Dallas Venture Capital leading the investment. The deal values the four-year-old startup at about $100 million, including the new funding.
Companies are nowadays spending heavily on GPUs to power AI applications, but running those models reliably and economically at scale remains a challenge. Different workloads demand distinct trade-offs between speed, cost, and performance. Deploying and operating AI models to meet business requirements often also requires complex adjustments. Simplismart says its software automates much of that work, tailoring how models run on existing computing infrastructure instead of requiring customers to manage those configurations themselves.
“Nobody actually needs the fastest or the cheapest inference,” Amritanshu Jain (pictured above, left), co-founder and CEO of Simplismart, said in an interview. He added that companies instead need to run AI models at speeds and costs that make sense for their specific applications.
Simplismart’s software sits between AI models and the computing infrastructure they run on and adjusts how models are deployed and managed to meet customers’ requirements. It says it can optimize factors such as how quickly a model responds, how many requests it handles, and how much computing power it consumes, helping companies get more out of their existing GPU stack.
The Bengaluru-based startup offers companies a way to deploy and run AI models through its own platform or within their existing cloud and on-premises infrastructure. It also provides tools to fine-tune models, automatically scale computing resources as demand changes, and monitor performance. Additionally, Simplismart allows cloud providers to build and operate their own AI inference services on GPU infrastructure using its software.
Simplismart says it helped AI video-generation platform InVideo cut its GPU serving costs by 56% using its software. The startup also works with AI video companies HeyGen and Higgsfield, as well as enterprise AI startup Ema, among others. Moreover, Indian cloud provider Yotta uses Simplismart’s technology to power the serverless AI inference service within its Shakti Studio platform.
Simplismart’s annualized revenue run rate has grown 14-fold over the past six months to an eight-figure sum, Jain told TechCrunch. The figure is based on recent customer usage rather than contracted recurring revenue and excludes revenue passed through to infrastructure providers, the company said. He did not disclose the exact figure.
More than half of Simplismart’s revenue comes from the U.S., despite the startup having more customers in India, Jain said.
Alongside its investment, Nvidia has been working with Simplismart on technical integrations, including around its Dynamo inference software, Jain told TechCrunch. The collaboration involves Simplismart’s engineers and Nvidia’s solutions architects, while Nvidia has also helped introduce the startup to potential customers and partners, Jain stated.
Interestingly, the investment presents an apparent paradox as Nvidia, the dominant supplier of AI chips, is backing software that can help companies run some workloads with fewer GPUs. Jain, however, argued that making AI inference more efficient could ultimately benefit Nvidia by making its hardware more attractive to customers and encouraging wider adoption of AI applications.
Simplismart is serving customers in an increasingly crowded market for AI inference software, competing with offerings from Nvidia itself, as well as major cloud providers and hyperscalers including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. A growing number of startups are also developing tools to make AI models faster and cheaper to run as there is growing demand in this segment, driven by rising demand for AI applications and the need to make better use of expensive GPU resources.
“Where we tend to win is where people have to be more stringent on their SLAs [service-level agreements] and TCO [total cost of ownership],” Jain said, referring to demanding performance requirements and tight cost constraints. Unlike rivals that offer preset options for faster or cheaper inference, Simplismart aims to find a balance tailored to each customer’s needs, he said.
Founded in 2022 by former Oracle engineer Jain and former Google engineer Devansh Ghatak (pictured above, right), Simplismart grew out of the pair’s experience building and deploying machine-learning systems. The two met while studying at BITS Pilani, and the startup now employs 58 people, Jain said.
Simplismart plans to use the new funding to expand its presence in the U.S., grow its team, and invest further in developing its inference software. Jain told TechCrunch that the U.S. remains a key market for the startup as it looks to build on its existing customer base there.
The funding announcement follows a
report
by Indian English daily The Economic Times that Simplismart was in talks to raise $40 million to $50 million at a valuation of $300 million to $400 million. Asked about the report, Jain declined to comment, saying the startup was not actively fundraising. He added that the Series B was closed and would not be extended.

The always-on AI personal assistant, which keeps working in the background even when you aren’t asking it to, is this year’s answer to the question of how people will actually use deep learning models. The startup Instinct became an overnight sensation, and Meta put the full force of its marketing behind its assistant, Muse.
OpenAI wasn’t going to be left out. The company
released dots
, its assistant offering, at its developer day in late September. Alexander Embiricos, who leads OpenAI’s enterprise product team, joined us at
TechCrunch Disrupt
this month to explain where the product came from — starting with the question of why so many companies seem to be turning to cutesy mascots as avatars for their trillion-parameter matrix multiplication machines.
“There’s kind of this convergent evolution happening,” Embiricos said of the efforts to build AI assistants. “As we were working on the product, we realized if we could frame this as, it’s an entity and it’s a single conversation, not many different conversations….it starts to become intuitive.”
The assistant is available in the ChatGPT desktop and mobile apps to subscribers on the Pro tier or higher, with plans starting at $100 a month. Once it is connected to your calendar, email, computer and other tools, the agent tries to help you get your work done.
Embiricos points out that you could achieve much of dots’ functionality with Open AI’s Codex app, its coding tool, released at the beginning of this year. But that requires more work and hand-holding. He recalled celebrating when his wife started leaving her computer on all night so that her agents could keep working.
“On the product team, what I think about is, how do we make this intuitive and useful to people?” he told Disrupt attendees. “A lot of that isn’t building some new piece of tech into the product; it’s how you frame it to the user and how it feels.”
The path from chatbot to coding tool to personal assistant
Making the technology feel intuitive meant repackaging the functionality of the company’s models into something more accessible, a path it was already on as it
spun ChatGPT Work
out of the agentic coding tools it had built for software engineers. Even the name — a play on the negative space inside of OpenAI’s logo — is intended “to feel like just something that could eventually be ubiquitous.” (Asked when he learned that rival AI entrepreneur Elon Musk owns the dot.com URL, Embiricos said, “I found out very late.”)
The idea of a persistent agent is that it doesn’t need prompting. For OpenAI, that means more token usage, and for users, a more pro-active assistant “that’s sort of thinking about you and thinking how to help you,” as Embiricos put it.
In our testing, the assistant’s ability to think ahead is apparent and often useful, but it isn’t quite there yet. It will flag calendar conflicts and upcoming deadlines, but not necessarily in the most timely fashion.
“The first time it told me about one of those [conflicts] — this is like early in development — it told me three minutes before the thing,” Embiricos says of his dot. “It’s like, ‘Hey, this thing is coming up. You might want to do something about it.’ I only have three minutes!”
Embiricos expects the timing to improve over time, but the proactive approach is key to the product. “I was hearing about an engineer at a drone delivery startup, and they were saying, ‘We had this outage, and by the time I noticed that the outage was going on, my dot had already noticed the outage was happening, had already analyzed the outage, and had come to me with useful information for how we could resolve the outage.’”
Giving dot the keys
As with most AI agent use cases, there’s a tension between the personal information an AI model needs to be useful and exactly how much personal data you are exposing to a software company. Muse has been criticized for
the profiles it builds
of your family and friends, which the software uses to know, say, what kind of restaurant you might want to go to with a specific pal, but could also add incredible value to Meta’s advertising business. Does dots collect similar data?
“Yes, we have a thing that we built into dots, which we call proactive research,” Embiricos said. “On a cadence, it will think about what it knows about you, what is the conversation that it’s had, and then what have you given it access to that it can think about, and then it will go and research, ‘What could I do to be more helpful to you?’ And then, basically, it will propose that.”
It’s difficult to separate the data needs of the agent from that of its parent corporation. Hark, a startup developing its own AI personal assistant, is explicit in pointing out that it doesn’t collect data to fuel an advertising business the way that OpenAI and Meta do.
With dots, OpenAI says that the agent has the same privacy controls as ChatGPT itself: Users can turn off model training (stopping OpenAI from using their conversations to improve its AI), and control which resources it accesses within your computer and how. Still, those controls aren’t granular and the app can be pushy. For example, it refuses to accept read-only access to cloud drives.
“What I think we need to do is basically build out super, super, super granular controls,” Embiricos said, but he pointed to the model’s intelligence and discretion as the other side of this coin.
“This is actually something we kind of got some flack about when we launched,” Embiricos said. “We had really conservative defaults over what the agent would do, and it would ask for permission a lot. I remember knowing that we were going to see that feedback, but thinking, ‘This is okay, we can tune that over time.’”
Can personal AI agents scale?
The other big question about AI agents is whether they can scale. They’re fun when only a few people have them, and stories of agents snagging hard-to-get reservations abound. But businesses don’t necessarily like dealing with agents and might not be equipped to. People certainly don’t like dealing with them (note: stop having your AI agents pitch me), and Embiricos is among those people. He also has a human assistant because  OpenAI’s corporate partners want to interact with a person, he said, adding, “I personally never intend to have a meeting with someone else’s agent.”
If the AI industry is right that agents are our future, can we get there without overwhelming the infrastructure that our world currently runs on, from businesses and websites to payment networks?
“At OpenAI…we’re not always moving the fastest in terms of shipping the next ability for the agent to work with the world,” he said. “When we do, we’re doing it really closely in collaboration with the rest of the ecosystem. I probably can’t say too much here, but we’re deep in lots of conversations with payment processors.”
Letting an AI assistant spend money through partnerships with payment companies would be a potentially lucrative first for OpenAI, but also a big ask for consumers. Giving an assistant access to my email inbox already feels like a big ask, but my bank account is off limits. For now.

Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
Expert ‘shepherds’ will decide how best to share the latest breakthroughs in computer science and physics.
Expert ‘shepherds’ will decide how best to share the latest breakthroughs in computer science and physics.
by
Robert Hart
Oct 27, 2026, 8:48 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Part Of
All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics
see all updates
Robert Hart
is a London-based reporter at
The Verge
covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for
Forbes
.
On Monday, OpenAI
announced
impressive
breakthroughs
in mathematics, computer science, and physics, along with what the company says is an evolving approach to communicating its findings. But despite its apparent course correction, researchers who spoke to
The Verge
are growing increasingly tired of the company’s antics.
It has been a turbulent few months between OpenAI and mathematicians, who are still grappling with the hundreds of preprints
unceremoniously dumped on them
at the start of October. This time, OpenAI says it is working with expert “shepherds” to decide how best to share its latest breakthroughs.
Related
‘Pure insanity’: Mathematicians will need years to make sense of OpenAI’s latest drop
The AI takeover of mathematics has begun
OpenAI just wants to win
All three results concern some of the most consequential unsolved problems in mathematics, computer science, and physics. Some extend OpenAI’s previous work and others break new ground. Following advice from OpenAI’s “shepherds,” each has a different release strategy. For the mathematics result, OpenAI released the AI-generated output, “leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.” For its computer science finding, OpenAI will also assemble an external group of researchers “to explain the result.” Physics, meanwhile, has not been released at all, and OpenAI said it will “defer” to an external group of experts about how to release the materials.
The mathematics result appears striking. It purports to resolve the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions. Roughly speaking, the problem asks how little space is needed to
rotate a needle or pencil
in every direction. A proof of the three-dimensional version was among the achievements for which NYU mathematician Hong Wang was
awarded
a prestigious Fields Medal earlier this year. Brown University mathematics professor Brendan Hassett told
The Verge
OpenAI’s claim “looks well supported,” though he stressed he had not yet checked the Lean formalization, a means of computationally verifying results.
The physics result explores the Standard Model, the most successful and complete theoretical framework in physics. It concerns quantum chromodynamics, which describes the strong nuclear force, one of nature’s four fundamental forces (alongside gravitational force, electromagnetic force, and weak nuclear force) and its relationship to Yang-Mills theory, a cornerstone of modern particle physics. Yang-Mills theory is also at the heart of one of the seven
Millennium Prize problems
in mathematics, though OpenAI’s work does not address the unresolved “mass gap.”
The final result claims to disprove the exponential time hypothesis, a widely held assumption in theoretical computer science that certain problems cannot be solved substantially faster than brute-force approaches. It is closely related to P versus NP, another Millennium Prize problem and one of the field’s biggest unsolved problems, which asks whether problems whose solutions can be easily checked are also easy to solve.
Given the varying levels of disclosure and the complexity of evaluating such work, it is difficult for researchers to fully judge the company’s findings. Even with all of the information, doing so would take time. But experts who spoke to
The Verge
said there are good reasons to take the results seriously, variously describing them as “huge,” “major breakthroughs,” and “significant.”
“It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them.”
But researchers’ excitement about the science was tempered by exasperation with OpenAI’s conduct, a familiar feeling after months of what they describe as an exhausting barrage of AI-generated findings. Many were eager for the wider community to get on with the arduous task of scrutinizing the AI lab’s findings and questioned why OpenAI was putting up additional barriers by handpicking experts to oversee the process.
Most experts
The Verge
spoke to welcomed OpenAI’s decision to consult outside researchers, but argued that publicly announcing results should also mean making that work available for anyone to scrutinize. “I am fine with them releasing the problems as they did today,” said Constantin Kogler, a researcher at the Institute for Advanced Study, welcoming the more manageable batch of three results compared with the hundreds released previously. But he questioned the decision to restrict access to experts of OpenAI’s choosing. “It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them,” he said.
Related
OpenAI keeps bulldozing mathematicians
OpenAI wants to consult elite mathematicians about how to not fumble again
Mathematicians want proof OpenAI didn’t use their work
“The fact that they handpick the group is a disaster,” Andreas Karch, a physics professor at the University of Texas at Austin, told
The Verge
. “The large labs have enough power as it is. They should not be picking winners and losers.” Karch initially suggested selecting researchers through a “competitive process,” though he acknowledged it would likely produce a similar group, which he described as “first rate.” Later, he questioned why OpenAI “can’t release the proof now,” in addition to appointing its team of experts. “This would democratize access while still showing that they care about making the results meaningful and understandable,” he said.
“My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset.”
It is exactly the kind of gatekeeping the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), a group of experts OpenAI had
previously pledged to consult
on how to share its findings,
warned
against just a day before the announcement. “We recommend that AI companies do not adopt this practice,” they said, arguing that selecting certain people to receive the output first is “unnecessary,” borrows the reputation of selected researchers, and risks unequal access, biased selection, and delays, among other issues. Instead, they recommended that AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with formalized proofs and information on how the problems were chosen, and provide funding and other support for people working on understanding the results.
Following the publication of the latest results, AGMAI urged OpenAI to “make public without delay the natural-language and Lean outputs behind its announced” results in physics:
”While these are central questions in physics, they are also important questions in mathematics. The existence of quantum Yang–Mills theory is part of a Millennium Prize problem and the construction of interacting quantum field theories in four dimensions has been a goal of mathematical physics for decades.
We have great respect for the scientists asked by OpenAI to lead this work. But as we explained in
our recent statement
, understanding should develop in the open, with everyone given the same access. OpenAI have said they delayed release until the Lean formalization was complete. By their own account this is now complete, so there is no scientific reason for delaying the release any further.”
Making the findings openly available could also lead to better science and encourage wider adoption of new tools like AI, Hassett said. “Having many groups around the world wrestle with these results supports rapid adoption of new tools by those that would like to use them,” he said.
”Fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution ... the papers are difficult to read and verify.”
Finding a way to communicate with researchers in the fields OpenAI is increasingly encroaching on that satisfies everyone may be impossible. The company says it is experimenting with different approaches and acknowledges that each has tradeoffs. “My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset,” said Stanford mathematician Jared Duker Lichtman. “So it’s just a question of finding the least offensive option.”
Xiaoyu He, a mathematics professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology, thinks the problem is deeper than how OpenAI chooses to announce its findings. ”The results are very impressive,” he said, “but I think they are making a show of trying to be responsible and thoughtful about how they release results while not being able to change the main issues: that fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution, and that the papers are difficult to read and verify.”
