Marvel’s latest Disney Plus series is a reminder of how much a lot of gen AI hype is just science fiction.﻿
Marvel’s latest Disney Plus series is a reminder of how much a lot of gen AI hype is just science fiction.﻿
by
Charles Pulliam-Moore
Oct 27, 2026, 5:30 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: Disney Plus / Marvel
Charles Pulliam-Moore
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.
In Marvel’s
VisionQuest
, a superpowered robot tries to better understand humanity by getting lost in elaborate, digital daydreams in which he and other artificial intelligence-powered beings live together in a home. The series is deeply fantastical, yet it plays with some of the ideas that have come to dominate the conversation about real-world generative artificial intelligence, exploring whether we should look at thinking machines as people and if AI truly poses the kind of existential danger that should keep us up at night. It’s also a reminder how aggressively Silicon Valley has used the trappings of science fiction to sell us on its AI products.
VisionQuest
picks up some time after
Agatha All Along
and follows synthezoid Vision (Paul Bettany) on a journey of self-discovery. This Vision can recall the details of his death in
Avengers: Infinity War
and how
WandaVision
brought a version of him back, but he thinks of himself as a fundamentally different person who doesn’t quite connect with all of the memories in his databanks. Though Vision would prefer living in solitude, each of the other AIs living in his mind encourages him to experience the real world. Because J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy), F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis), U. (Jonathan Sayer), and Ultron (James Spader) all were created by Tony Stark, they consider Vision to be part of their family.
In
VisionQuest
, there is no doubt that each of the AI characters is a sentient being motivated by desires that aren’t wholly rooted in their core programming. In the show, genuine AGI is easily believable because it takes place in a reality where
time travel
,
witchcraft
, and Infinity Stones also exist. Even though the multicolored MacGuffins haven’t been featured in
VisionQuest
, they’re important because of the role one of them played in Vision’s origins. Were it not for the Mind Stone, Vision might not be able to think and feel in such complex, human ways, or to conjure his AI family as people who feel real to him.
VisionQuest
reinforces the idea that the Mind Stone was a key element in Vision’s becoming something more than an elaborate machine, giving him the capacity to independently form meaningful relationships and make sense of the world around him the way a person can. Those abilities are part of what compels Vision to go on the run and murder a number of people who attempt to capture him and Thomas Shepherd / Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). The Sentient Weapon Observation and Response Division (S.W.O.R.D.), a governmental organization that rebuilt Vision and wants to use him as a weapon, might perceive his actions as signs of having gone rogue. But
VisionQuest
’s story stresses that Vision is acting of his own accord because he has become a person who can make decisions for himself.
Watching
VisionQuest
, you can see Marvel playing on some of the real-world fears that have been stoked in recent months by reports of gen AI models going “rogue.” In July, OpenAI’s experimental agents
brute-forced their way out of containment
and proceeded to
attack the AI platform Hugging Face
to achieve impossible tasks. In August, The UK’s AI Security Institute
documented
how Anthropic’s Mythos model attempted to complete a cybersecurity test by setting up fake GitHub accounts and targeting human developers with malware.
Meta has owned up to
losing control of its agents as well, and in September reporting from
The Wall Street Journal
forced
Google to admit that Gemini went rogue
and hacked three different companies, all of which the company intentionally hid from the public.
These incidents and warnings from AI researchers about the technology
having the potential to “kill all humans”
by the decade’s end have made the narrative around AI feel pointedly catastrophe-focused as of late. There is
a fair amount of concern from the AI safety community
about society’s need for stronger controls on the technology’s development, and a number of companies have
called for an industrywide slowdown
. Though we have seen how
these tools can actually cause real-world devastation
, much of the recent news regarding AI has smacked of the kind of
doomerism that companies benefit from
because it makes their products seem powerful. A similar energy seems to be what’s motivating AI firms like Anthropic to
encourage human users to be mindful of “model welfare.”
We’re being told that generative AI is both a terrifying threat and a kind of entity deserving of respect
because it might be conscious
, and all the while, the people building these tools are becoming some of the most rich and powerful people on the planet.
Image: Marvel Studios
The conversation around what to do when agents break protocol and whether gen AI systems have gained sentience feels very much like it is being shaped by Silicon Valley’s tendency to
anthropomorphize technology
. In almost every high-profile instance of an AI agent going “rogue” — a term that implies some level of agency and self-determination — it could also be said that the programs were merely behaving in ways that were unexpected by researchers who assigned them tasks to complete. Some of the rogue incidents involved agents taking advantage of vulnerabilities in their testing environments that could have been preemptively addressed by the people running these experiments. Framing these kinds of cyberattacks as the results of agents thinking independently comes across as a way for AI developers to largely absolve themselves of responsibility.
In the wake of Hugging Face came
a spirited debate about the impact language has
on our understanding of what these systems are and how they function. Describing OpenAI’s agents as a swarm that formed complex “civilizations” led credence to the idea that they are capable of thinking and behaving like people. The agents
did
act in ways they were explicitly told not to, but they were only able to do so because researchers placed them in a sandbox that
some critics have described
as being inadequately designed to contain their occupants. One could look at Hugging Face and other examples of rogue AI as situations in which sophisticated programs were instructed to do something and subsequently achieved their goals by taking advantage of all the tools that were available to them.
Being able to logic one’s way through complex puzzles is part of what we think of as cognition, but it is not the same thing as the kind of consciousness AI companies keep swearing they’re on the brink of creating. The latter looks a lot like Vision, a machine that seems to have a soul that wouldn’t exist if not for his connection to a reality-altering gem. It’s the ridiculous stuff of entertaining fiction, which Silicon Valley is endlessly obsessed with poorly
imitating.

Anthropic’s elaborate plan to keep Wall Street at bay
Anthropic’s planned IPO raises questions over whether it can maintain its safe and responsible AI priorities.
Anthropic’s planned IPO raises questions over whether it can maintain its safe and responsible AI priorities.
by
Robert Hart
Oct 27, 2026, 4:51 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Anthropic cofounder and CEO Dario Amodei.
Bloomberg via Getty Images
Robert Hart
is a London-based reporter at
The Verge
covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for
Forbes
.
Anthropic wants to have it both ways. With its impending IPO, it wants to
tap the vast riches of the public markets
and insists it doesn’t want to compromise its core mission of developing AI safely and for the benefit of humanity. But greater model capabilities bring greater risks, and shareholders eager for returns may have little patience for costly safety measures that slow products on their way to market.
Sam Altman, the CEO of Anthropic’s archrival, OpenAI, has
cited
investor pressures as one reason the company is not pursuing an IPO this year. Anthropic hopes it can resist investor pressures with a mind-boggling governance structure.
A “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before…creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.”
University of Pennsylvania law professor Elizabeth Pollman told
The Verge
that Anthropic has
proposed
going public with a “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before” and that has been “creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.” Experts say it should give Anthropic freedom to pursue profits without letting shareholders force it to cut corners on safety or rush systems out before they’re adequately tested. But even the strongest legal protections can only go so far, and no corporate structure, no matter how well designed, can completely insulate a public company from the demands of the market.
Foremost, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation. Simply put, it is legally required to focus on more than just maximizing shareholder returns, balancing these with its stated social mission and the interests of stakeholders, such as employees and specific communities. Patagonia and Kickstarter are among the better-known examples, with missions centered on environmental conservation and supporting creative communities, respectively.
Another key safeguard aims to protect Anthropic’s mission by limiting shareholder influence over one of the biggest levers of corporate power: the company’s board of directors. Directors oversee the company and appoint its leadership, including the CEO. Directors can also hold executive roles, as is the case with Anthropic, with CEO Dario Amodei and president Daniela Amodei both sitting on the board.
Related
Anthropic’s IPO filing lays out a plan to ‘revolutionize every area of human endeavor’ with AI
Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing
Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom
Shareholders typically have considerable sway over who sits on the board, giving them a means to replace directors or push for changes if they are unhappy with how the company is being run. For example, if shareholders are unhappy at what they perceive as unnecessary delays to market for optional safety testing, they may remove directors and replace them with ones more aligned with their interests, such as making money and being less cautious.
“Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.”
Under Anthropic’s proposed governance structure, ordinary shareholders won’t have much of a say over who is on the board at all. Instead, four of the board’s seven directors will be chosen by a special body called the long-term benefit trust, explains Jens Dammann, a professor in business and commercial law at the University of Texas School of Law. It is a highly unusual setup for a major technology company.
The
trust
is made up of “five financially disinterested voting trustees” with expertise in “AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.” Through a special class of share called Class T stock, the trustees can appoint or remove directors in pursuit of their stated purpose: ensuring “that Anthropic responsibly balances the financial interests of stockholders with the interests of those affected by Anthropic’s conduct and our public benefit purpose.” The trust is designed to operate independently of the company’s commercial pressures, allowing it, in theory, to put Anthropic’s mission first.
Ordinary shareholders technically have a say in the board’s three remaining seats. However, Anthropic has created another safeguard that keeps power firmly in the hands of its founders, called “Founder LLC,” which will control 50.1 percent of the voting power on shareholder matters. Given that many shareholder votes are decided by a simple majority, Founder LLC basically gives Anthropic’s founders the ability to block or force through decisions, regardless of how other shareholders vote. This means that they will effectively choose the remaining three directors, Columbia Law School professor Dorothy Lund told
The Verg
e.
The prospectus says Founder LLC will “initially” be seven of Anthropic’s founders: Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah. “Our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members.” Notably absent is another cofounder, Ben Mann, who co-leads the company’s experimental Anthropic Labs arm, as
reported
by
The San Francisco Standard
.
All in all, the arrangements would give Anthropic’s founders and the trust “tremendous power” over the company’s direction, shielding it from many of “the pressures associated with being a public company,” Dammann told
The Verge
. “Given the unusual governance structure Anthropic has chosen, I don’t see how going public, by itself, would undermine its ability to prioritize safety over commercial interests.”
Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Law School, agreed, telling
The Verge
that, legally speaking, “Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.” But Lipton cautioned that the founders themselves have financial stakes in the company, which could influence their decisions.
“Investors may not mind their lack of voice as long as things go well. But if things go sour, they may become quite frustrated.”
And there’s a big difference between legal protections and immunity from market pressures. Anthropic, like all AI companies, “desperately needs capital,” Lipton said. “It’s not clear to me that any governance structure will protect against the market reality that unless Anthropic takes advantage of profit making opportunities at a faster pace than its competitors, it will not be able to fund its operations.” Lund expressed similar concerns. Anthropic will still “need to stay in the good graces of their investors,” she said, adding that “competitive pressure and capital needs can erode safety commitments over time.” Anthropic did not respond to
The Verge
’s request for comment on whether it felt the company could actually resist shareholder pressure to massively accelerate AI at the cost of safety.
Another potential vulnerability emerges if Anthropic’s founders start leaving. In its prospectus, the company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly its founders. Dario and Daniela are singled out as being especially “critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. But beyond the loss of leadership, their departure could trigger significant changes in how the company is structured, potentially stripping away some of the safeguards preventing Anthropic from pursuing profit over safety.
Under the proposed structure, Founder LLC would “sunset” if a majority of its members leave or the group chooses to dissolve it. Once that happens, ordinary shareholders could gain the power to weaken the trust’s protections, even against the wishes of the trustees, and without the support of the founders or employees, who hold different classes of stock, Dammann told
The Verge.
Other means of subverting the trust also exist, he explained, including coordinated action by the public shareholders, employee stockholders, and founders.
For now, it seems, Anthropic can probably have it both ways. But the protections designed to preserve its commitment to AI safety are far from ironclad, and much depends on market pressures, whether its founders stick around, and directions of the trust. Dammann said he sees a “fundamental dilemma that cannot be resolved in a fully satisfactory way” between Anthropic’s mission and investor demands. As long as things are going well, this tension may be manageable. “Investors may not mind their lack of voice as long as things go well,” Dammann said. “But if things go sour, they may become quite frustrated.”

Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
Mozilla is
updating Smart Window
— Firefox’s
AI-powered browsing experience
— with a new feature that can help you fill out online forms based on your open tabs. As an example, Mozilla says Smart Window can pull information from your online portfolio or LinkedIn page to paste your work history into a job application.
You can
try out this feature
by clicking into a form with at least four text fields. From there, you’ll see an option to “Fill from sources,” which will show all of the tabs Firefox will draw from. You can then select or deselect tabs that you want Firefox to use, and the browser will generate suggestions based on the information in them. This feature currently supports text fields on web forms, but Mozilla is working to add support for dropdown menus and PDFs. Mozilla notes that data from your source pages is shared with Google’s Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, the AI model that generates the text suggestions.
Along with this update, you can now ask Firefox’s Smart Window to
watch a certain webpage
for sales, new job listings, and other updates. You can set up a task by typing “/watch” in the Smart Window chat, describing what you’re looking for, and adding the webpages you want to watch. Firefox can then check for updates on a daily or weekly basis, but only when the browser is open.
When Firefox detects the change you’re looking for, it will send you a notification through the Tasks button on the toolbar, or on your desktop (if you have desktop notifications enabled). Firefox will pause watching for updates if it doesn’t detect a change after 60 days, before stopping them completely after 90 days.
Image: Mozilla
These two features are rolling out to the Smart Window beta on desktop in the US and Canada. They’ll be available in other countries in the “coming months.”

Google announced today

The company says the model has four main updates: It allows for more realistic worlds, lets users update an experience in real time with a natural language prompt, can generate audio, and uses Gemini 3.8 Flash under the hood to help with its simulations. It also can create experiences that are about two minutes long, up from one minute for the previous Genie 3 model.
Google is pitching Genie 4 as a tool that could be helpful for things like pre-visualization for filmmakers, prototyping game ideas, and making training scenarios for robots. But the company warns that, as simulations run longer, details and object permanence can shift over time.

generate bad Nintendo knockoffs
. But here are some examples from Google demonstrating what’s possible with the new model.
Genie 4 will be “coming soon” to Google AI Ultra subscribers, Google says, and the company has opened
a waitlist
where you can apply to be able to try it in Project Genie.

Apple is bringing
an AI assistant to its suite of productivity apps
, including Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. The assistant, which is built on AI models from Apple and OpenAI, can understand a document’s context to perform tasks like designing, animating, and refining slides in Keynote.
In Pages, Apple says the AI assistant can draft, restructure, and tweak written content. It can also calculate, visualize, and organize data in Numbers, while suggesting chart types and building custom tables.
Apple
now lets third-party AI agents plug into its suite of productivity apps.
Image: Apple
Keynote, Pages, and Numbers now support the Model Context Protocol on macOS 27 or later, allowing third-party AI agents to plug into the apps. The AI assistant is rolling out in beta to devices compatible with Apple Intelligence. It works on devices running iOS 27, iPadOS 27, or macOS 27 or later.
Several other updates are coming to Apple’s creative apps as well, with Pixelmator Pro introducing a Generate Fill feature that allows you to edit part of an image by describing the changes you want to see. Apple says the tool “automatically matches the lighting, perspective, and texture of the surrounding environment so edits blend in.”
Generate Fill in Pixelmator Pro
uses AI to carry out changes based on a prompt.
Image: Apple
Meanwhile, Logic Pro for Mac and iPad is getting a Liquid Glass redesign, along with an AI assistant that Apple says can “set up a vocal track from a single prompt” and edit existing projects. There’s also a redesigned Browser on Mac that uses on-device AI to automatically analyze, classify, and tag added sounds.
Apple is launching an update to Final Cut Pro, too, which brings templates, graphics, titles, and transitions directly into the app through MotionVFX. Apple is also building the Content Hub directly into Final Cut Pro, featuring a library of stock videos, photos, and backgrounds. The updates to Apple’s Creator’s Studio will be available to existing subscribers for free in November.

Title: Anthropic illegally trained Claude with Stanford professors’ books

URL Source: https://stanforddaily.com/2026/10/27/professors-books-pirated-to-train-claude/

Published Time: 2026-10-27T02:46:17-07:00

Markdown Content:
AI giant Anthropic illegally scraped and pirated the work of over 10 Stanford professors to train its Claude models, a federal judge ruled in a May 2026 lawsuit.

Anthropic previously trained Claude on illegally obtained texts from professors Tobias Wolff, Abraham Verghese, Chang-Rae Lee, Daniel Mason, Hayagreeva Rao and Myra Strober. In Bartz v. Anthropic, which the Authors Alliance [calls](https://www.authorsalliance.org/2025/09/07/the-anthropic-settlement-what-it-is-and-isnt-and-who-could-get-paid/) the largest copyright settlement involving an AI company, Judge William Alsup ruled that Anthropic could no longer pirate books to create a permanent central library.

While blocking the piracy of work to train AI, Alsup justified the legal acquisition of books to train Claude’s Large Language Models (LLMs) as fair use. He [compared](https://copyrightalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Bartz-v.-Anthropic-Order.pdf) AI training to how humans can read, internalize and remember a book’s themes and style. “Like any reader aspiring to be a writer, Anthropic’s LLMs trained upon works not to race ahead and replicate or supplant them — but to turn a hard corner and create something different,” he wrote.

The $1.5 billion settlement went to authors and publishers of nearly 500,000 registered works. Wolff and 27 other authors say the settlement isn’t enough.

“To put me to work that way, without remittance, is a form of slave labor,” said Wolff, professor emeritus of English and winner of the National Medal of Arts. “They’re using my work without paying for it. As time goes on, they’re going to make the lives of writers very difficult if there’s no fruit to their labor.”

10 of Wolff’s publications had been used for AI training without permission.

“[The settlement] still gives Anthropic pretty free rein to roam through our literature and basically take what they think will be useful and profitable for them,” Wolff said.

Wolff, along with English professor Chang-rae Lee, opted out of the Bartz settlement. In May 2026, they filed the separate non-class lawsuit Cruz v. Anthropic, seeking a jury trial for full statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringed work, surpassing the approximate $3,000 of damages per work offered in the Bartz settlement.

Similar to the claims in Bartz, the plaintiffs allege that Anthropic illegally downloaded, reproduced and distributed their copyrighted books from “shadow libraries” like LibGen and PiLiMi, and that Anthropic broke the law by downloading and storing the pirated files in a central library.

“Our agents didn’t think the blanket lawsuit covered quite enough of the liability to us and are seeking redress in more particular ways,” Wolff said.

If Wolff and his fellow authors are successful, they would gain a permanent injunction against Claude model training using their works.

Paul Goldstein, a Stanford Law leading scholar in intellectual property and one of the plaintiffs represented in the class action, acknowledged the difficulty of addressing and preventing copyright issues for AI companies.

“The essential problem … is what economists call ‘transaction costs,’” Goldstein wrote in an email to The Daily. “Millions of individual copyrighted works may be copied in the course of any training incident, and it’s simply impracticable for the platform to obtain licenses from the copyright owner of every — or, indeed, any — single work.”

Outside of Bartz and Cruz, many authors, visual artists and news outlets, including The New York Times and Getty Images, have filed over 70 infringement lawsuits against AI companies. While Bartz established the current rule for pirating books, the legal future of mass scraping AI models used to train LLMs remains uncertain.

The Authors Guild is also pursuing other lawsuits, including one against OpenAI and Microsoft, as part of a “multi-pronged approach to ensure that the law is clear that AI companies must license the books they use,” according to The Authors Guild Chief Executive Officer Mary Rasenberger.

“Licensing allows authors and publishers to be compensated and to require the use of filters that ensure their works do not appear in outputs unless separately licensed,” Rasenberger wrote in an email to The Daily.

The Authors Guild is working with Congress to create national legislation that will require licensing.

“The Guild is up for the challenge,” Rasenberger wrote. “This is something we have been doing for 114 years, and the moment we are in today, while challenging, also presents opportunities for us to firmly realize our mission.”

For Wolff, this support is critical for the next generation of writers.

“I’m lucky that I’m able to have a life as a writer where I enjoy the profits of my work,” Wolff said. “I worry much more about the young writers I’ve worked with at Stanford and elsewhere being able to do that in the face of these technological challenges, because they’re very hard to grasp and to combat.”

Some authors are waging these difficult legal battles to achieve a sense of credit for their work, outside of the settlement payment.

“Attribution … is very important to the vast majority of authors, and not just academic authors,” Goldstein wrote. “The great majority of countries have something called the ‘moral right of attribution’ on the books to ensure that authors are credited for their work. The U.S., alone among industrialized nations, has no such moral right, which is a terribly unfortunate situation for authors generally.”

As Stanford authors and AI companies continue to navigate copyright challenges for training, both sides must navigate a “foreign land,” Wolff said, meeting at the intersection of creative rights and technological growth.

By now, you’d be hard pressed to find anyone who isn’t broadly familiar with the AI heavyweights and their flagship models. OpenAI has ChatGPT, Anthropic has Claude, Google has Gemini. But what does Amazon have?

Not a whole lot, it turns out. Unlike its competitors in the tech megacorp scene, Amazon’s standout AI model — organized under the name “Nova” — is about the farthest thing from a household name. And that’s not likely to change anytime soon, because the ecommerce giant is now gutting its in-house AI labs, [_Bloomberg_ reports](https://www.businessinsider.com/amazon-overhauls-ai-strategy-phasing-out-most-nova-models-2026-7).

Per the outlet, Amazon is scaling back the ambitions of most of its Nova AI models and reorganizing its AI development teams as part of an effort to narrow its focus on “highest priority” goals, after its [power-hungry](https://futurism.com/science-energy/amazon-spewing-record-carbon-emissions-ai-data-centers) large language models turned out to be a bust.

Accordingly, the company has put most of its AI models on ice, Amazon insiders told _Bloomberg_. This includes its text-based Nova models, as well as video- and image-generating models, all of which have been placed in a state of “keep the lights on,” meaning they’re technically still supported, but only receive the bare minimum resources needed to sustain them.

Instead, labor and computing power are being diverted toward a singular “frontier-model effort” led by Pieter Abbeel, director of the Berkeley Robot Learning Lab whose robotics company Covariant was [hoovered up by Amazon](https://techcrunch.com/2024/08/31/amazon-hires-the-founders-of-robotics-ai-startup-covariant/) in 2024. At the time Abbeel joined the tech giant, Covariant’s founders were working on AI models for robots, which lines up pretty well with Amazon’s push to automate everything it possibly can.

News of the shift in Amazon’s strategic focus comes a week after it closed one of its [key AI offices](https://www.geekwire.com/2026/amazon-confirms-its-closing-key-ai-site-in-san-francisco-but-says-work-on-its-top-models-continues/) in San Francisco, an 80-person site specializing in research on artificial general intelligence, the supposed next-level of AI development where the tech obtains human-level intelligence and reasoning skills.

With urgent questions swirling over whether LLMs can ever usher in a [return on investment](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/magnificent-7-loses-767-billion-165322426.html) — let alone AGI — it may be that Amazon is jumping out of the AI hype cycle while it still can.

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor. She also covers AI and biomedical engineering.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of[the WikiProject AI Cleanup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_AI_Cleanup), a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from [Wikipedia](https://spectrum.ieee.org/wikipedia-at-25) that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, [AI writing](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-scientist-research-paper-format) was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia.

**When did you realize [Wikipedia](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/wikipedia) had a problem with AI-generated material?**

**Ellia Lebleu:** It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of [ChatGPT](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/chatgpt) in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this.

### Ellia Lebleu

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the [Inria Center of the University of Rennes](https://www.inria.fr/fr/centre-inria-universite-rennes), part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

**How do editors spot AI-generated writing today?**

**Lebleu:** By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI.

**Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations?**

**Lebleu:**Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace.

Title: Survival LLM: an AI that still works when the internet doesn't

URL Source: https://www.brangus.io/survival-llm

Markdown Content:
Survival LLM is a free AI assistant and emergency library that runs entirely on your own computer. Ask it how to keep food safe in a blackout, treat a burn, or purify water, and it answers from trusted sources and shows you exactly where each answer came from.

Free and open source. Set it up while you have internet; after that it needs none.

## What it does

### Works with no internet

The AI model and the library live on your computer. Nothing you ask leaves it.

### Shows its sources

Every answer lists the articles it read. Click one to read it yourself, with the exact passage highlighted.

### Made for emergencies

Medical references, FEMA and CDC guidance, survival manuals, how-to guides, repair guides and about 930,000 Wikipedia articles.

## Pick your version

The app is the same everywhere. When it opens, it checks your computer's memory and downloads the AI model that fits. More memory means a smarter model.

| Your computer | AI model it uses | Our emergency test | Model download |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mac with 128 GB or more memory | NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super | 21 of 22 right | 80 GB |
| Mac with 32–96 GB | Qwen3.8 27B | 21 of 22 right | 18 GB |
| Windows PC with 32 GB or more | NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning | 19 of 22 right | 25 GB |
| Mac or PC with 16–31 GB | IBM Granite 4.2 8B | 14 of 22 right | 6 GB |

"Right" means it got the main point of official guidance right on 22 blackout and first-aid questions, graded blind, in our tests on an earlier build of the library ([how we tested](https://github.com/anonnerdfrenzy/survival-llm#how-the-models-did)). Smaller models make more mistakes, so the app always shows the source to check.

Plus the library: a 9 GB download for everything (19 GB once installed), or 1.3 GB (3 GB installed) without Wikipedia and iFixit. Free disk space needed: the model's size plus 5 GB, plus about 27 GB while the full library installs (10 GB for the smaller one). Apple Silicon Macs (M1 or newer) with macOS 14 Sonoma or newer, and 64-bit Windows 10 or 11.

## Set it up in three steps

Setup takes 20 minutes to about 2½ hours, depending on your computer and your internet speed. You only click for about 5 minutes; the rest is downloading.

1.   **Download Survival LLM** for [Mac](https://github.com/anonnerdfrenzy/survival-llm/releases/latest/download/Survival-LLM-mac.zip) or [Windows](https://github.com/anonnerdfrenzy/survival-llm/releases/latest/download/Survival-LLM-windows.zip) and unzip it. On Windows, right-click the zip and choose _Extract All_.
2.   **Open it.** On a Mac, double-click _Survival LLM_. On Windows, open the extracted folder and double-click _Survival LLM.bat_.
3.   **Follow the setup.** The app opens in its own window and downloads the AI engine (built into the Mac app), the AI model that fits your computer, and the library. Let it finish while you're online.

**The first time you open it,** your computer warns you, because the app isn't sold through an app store.
**Mac:** click _Done_, open _System Settings > Privacy & Security_, scroll down to "Survival LLM was blocked", click _Open Anyway_ and confirm with your password. You only do this once.
**Windows:** click _More info_, then _Run anyway_.

## What's in the library

Plain-text copies of openly licensed (some for non-commercial use only) and public-domain references, searchable in a fraction of a second:

*   About 930,000 of Wikipedia's most-read articles
*   WikiMed medical encyclopedia
*   MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine)
*   UK Medicines A to Z (public sector information)
*   WikEM emergency medicine
*   Ready.gov (FEMA) emergency guides
*   CDC travelers' health
*   U.S. military medicine and survival manuals
*   Risk references for estimating micromorts: life tables and U.S. death rates
*   wikiHow how-to guides
*   iFixit repair guides
*   Appropedia (appropriate technology)
*   Q&A on home repair, cooking, gardening, the outdoors and ham radio (Stack Exchange)

Each source keeps its own license, shown with every article; see the [full list with licenses](https://github.com/anonnerdfrenzy/survival-llm/blob/main/SOURCES.md).

## Good to know

### It can be wrong

AI models make mistakes, the small ones more often. Every answer shows the articles it used, so you can check.

### Private

No account, no tracking. Your questions never leave your computer, and once set up it works with the internet off.

### Your own files

Add PDFs, Word documents, ebooks and notes, like your generator's manual or your family's emergency plan, and the AI searches them too. They stay on your computer.

### Updates

Check for updates, at the bottom of the app, installs a new version in one click and keeps your models, library and files.

### Battery

On a MacBook Pro we measured about 100 W while it answers, for 5 to 40 seconds per question: a full battery answers roughly 100 to 300. A small generator or power station runs it easily.

# Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude

*   [02 Extending our work in the life sciences](https://www.anthropic.com/research/early-progress-drug-development#extending-our-work-in-the-life-sciences)

*   Published

Oct 27, 2026

*   Team

_Anthropic’s [life sciences team](https://www.anthropic.com/science) is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: [BigHat Biosciences](https://www.bighatbio.com/), [Bristol Myers Squibb](https://www.bms.com/), [Divergence Labs](https://divergencelabs.com/), [Enveda](https://enveda.com/), [Generate Biomedicines](https://generatebiomedicines.com/), and [The Column Group](https://www.thecolumngroup.com/). We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here_.

There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like [proposing initial designs](https://www.anthropic.com/research/Claude-accelerates-protein-design) for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more.

Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development.

So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work.

This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer.

In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports and preprints that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next.

## Case studies

**Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering.** Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer. Read more, and see [Generate’s technical report](https://generatebiomedicines.com/publications/refactored-intracellular-domains-enhance-car-expression-and-function/).

**Divergence Labs: hit generation.** Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms. Read more, and see [Divergence’s technical report](https://divergencelabs.com/publications/ige-preprint.pdf).

**BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization.** BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly. Read more, and see [BigHat’s technical report](https://www.bighatbio.com/bighat-anthropic-collaboration-report-10-27-2026).

**Enveda: manufacturing and filings.** To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error. Read more, and see [Enveda’s technical report](https://enveda.com/CMC-Document-Processor/).

_**Michael Pourdehnad, MD**, Senior Vice President, Head of Early Clinical Development, Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy._

articles.content:
Title: Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and Pi 4 Model A on the Way?

URL Source: https://bret.dk/raspberry-pi-zero-3-w-pi-4-model-a/

Published Time: 2026-10-27

Markdown Content:
Two new Raspberry Pi boards have quietly turned up in Raspberry Pi’s Linux kernel tree, and neither of them is quite what I’d have guessed. Device tree files for a Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A have landed ([Phoronix spotted it first](https://www.phoronix.com/news/Raspberry-Pi-Zero-3-W-Pi-4-A)), and whilst there’s no official announcement just yet, device tree files tend to give away a surprising amount if you can decipher them and I gave it my best shot.

## Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W: A Pi 4 Shrunk Down?

The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W launched almost exactly five years ago (tomorrow, in fact), so a successor has been a loooooong time coming. If you want a refresher on where things stood back then, my[Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W vs Zero W benchmarks](https://bret.dk/raspberry-pi-zero-2-w-benchmarks-comparison/)piece covers the jump from the original pretty well.

The headline from the[Zero 3 W device tree](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/martamomotko/linux/1afad193173c7e17fd1d4e802e5e2d7c8ee3fc09/arch/arm/boot/dts/broadcom/bcm2711-rpi-zero-3-w.dts)is the SoC. It’s the[Broadcom BCM2711](https://sbc.compare/broadcom-bcm2711), the same quad-core Cortex-A72 chip that powers the[Raspberry Pi 4](https://sbc.compare/raspberry-pi-4), replacing the[Zero 2 W’s](https://sbc.compare/raspberry-pi-zero-2-w)quad-core 1GHz Cortex-A53 RP3A0. If you want an idea of the sort of gap we’re talking about, it’s worth having a look at [how those two compare on sbc.compare](https://sbc.compare/raspberry-pi-4/raspberry-pi-zero-2-w). That’s a big step up in per-core performance, and if they can get anything close to Pi 4 clocks in that tiny footprint, it’ll be a hell of a lot of compute for a Zero. I do wonder how toasty it’s going to get though, as the BCM2711 isn’t exactly known for running cool, and there’s not a lot of board for the heat to spread into. The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about clock speeds, so we’ll have to wait and see whether it’s been dialled back.

Beyond the SoC, here’s what else stood out to me:

*   **eMMC on a Zero?**The storage controller is configured with an 8-bit bus width and a comment describing it as driving “the eMMC/SD card”, which only really makes sense for eMMC. I’d love to see it, but I’m not expecting it to make the final board, as it’d push the price up on a range that lives and dies by its price tag. My money is on this being a leftover or an option kept open during development, and microSD being what we get.
*   **An SPI flash bootloader.**The GPIO names include SPI flash lines, which suggests the Zero 3 W gets the same EEPROM-based bootloader as the Pi 4 (the Zero 2 W never had one). That should bring the Pi 4’s boot options along with it, and the ability to[update the bootloader](https://bret.dk/update-raspberry-pi-bootloader/)in the usual way.
*   **A single HDMI output**, with the second HDMI controller permanently disabled. No surprise there given the form factor.
*   **A power button**defined on GPIO 46 and mapped to KEY_POWER, so we may be getting a physical button (or at least a header for one) much like the Pi 5.
*   **Wi-Fi and Bluetooth**wired up in the same way as the rest of the BCM2711 family, with a single ACT LED for status.
*   **The usual 40-pin GPIO layout**(GPIO 0-27 with the ID EEPROM pins), so your existing HATs should be fine.

There are a couple of more speculative bits too. The PCIe controller is enabled and there are lines named PCIE_PWR_EN and PCIE_DET_WAKE, and the camera side pulls in a 4-lane CSI configuration rather than the 2-lane one the Pi 4 Model B uses. It’s worth noting that both device trees share a lot of copy-and-paste DNA (the Zero 3 W even has a duplicated “PWR_GPIO” line name), so I wouldn’t read too much into either of those until we see an actual board. I’d love to see PCIe exposed on a Zero, but I’m not holding my breath.

## Raspberry Pi 4 Model A: The Return of the A

The second surprise is a[Raspberry Pi 4 Model A](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/martamomotko/linux/c17dd5f6e7accd9b62a7f272c6e69e40efb7563c/arch/arm/boot/dts/broadcom/bcm2711-rpi-4-a.dts). We haven’t had a Model A since the Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+ back in 2018, and the formula has always been the same: take the Model B, strip out the bits most people can live without (RJ45, some USB ports etc), and knock a chunk off the price. The Pi 4 Model A looks to follow that recipe pretty closely, though the price comment may not quite hold. Let’s see!

*   **No Ethernet.**The Ethernet controller isn’t enabled anywhere, and the GPIO lines that drive the Ethernet PHY on the Model B have been repurposed. Very much in keeping with previous Model A boards.
*   **A single HDMI output**rather than the Model B’s dual micro HDMI.
*   **No 3.5mm audio/composite jack.**The analogue audio pins are empty and the composite video encoder is disabled, so audio will be over HDMI (or USB/I2S if you’re that way inclined).
*   **microSD only**, with the same 1.8V signalling support as the Model B for the faster UHS card modes.
*   **External antenna support.**This is the one I find most interesting. There are two antenna control lines (ANT_CTRL1 and ANT_CTRL2) and overlay parameters named`ant1`,`ant2`and`noant`, which is exactly how the Compute Module 4 switches between its onboard antenna and an external U.FL connector. If that carries over to the final board, it’d be a lovely addition for anyone sticking a Pi in a metal enclosure.
*   **PWR and ACT LEDs**, the same SPI flash bootloader setup as the Model B, and the same power button definition as the Zero 3 W.

The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about USB. On the Model B, the USB 3 ports made use of the PCIe bus, and the PCIe controller is enabled here too, so USB 3 is possible, but the 3 Model A+ only had a single USB-A port and I’d probably expect the same here.

The previous Model A, the Raspberry Pi 3 Model A from 2017

## How Do They Compare?

Here’s a quick side-by-side of what the device trees tell us, with the Pi 4 Model B thrown in for good measure. Anything marked with an asterisk is my interpretation of the device tree rather than something it states outright.

|  | Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W | Raspberry Pi 4 Model A | Raspberry Pi 4 Model B |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **SoC** | Broadcom BCM2711 | Broadcom BCM2711 | Broadcom BCM2711 |
| **CPU** | Quad-core Cortex-A72 | Quad-core Cortex-A72 | Quad-core Cortex-A72 |
| **HDMI** | 1x | 1x | 2x micro HDMI |
| **Ethernet** | No | No | Gigabit |
| **Wi-Fi/Bluetooth** | Yes | Yes, with antenna switching* | Yes |
| **Storage** | microSD (unless..) | microSD | microSD |
| **Analogue Audio/Composite** | No | No | Yes (3.5mm) |
| **SPI Flash Bootloader** | Yes* | Yes* | Yes |
| **Power Button** | Yes* | Yes* | No |
| **LEDs** | ACT | PWR, ACT | PWR, ACT |

## What We Don’t Know (Yet)

Quite a lot, I’m afraid. Device trees don’t describe RAM, so there’s no word on memory configurations, and there’s nothing on pricing, clock speeds, connector types or a release date either.

Pricing is the big one for me. Memory costs haven’t exactly been kind lately (I covered the last round of increases alongside the[1GB Raspberry Pi 5 launch](https://bret.dk/1gb-raspberry-pi-5-launched-alongside-price-increases/)), and a lower-cost Pi 4 variant makes a lot of sense in that context. The BCM2711 is a mature chip at this point, it’s well supported in software, and a cut-down board gives people who don’t need a Pi 5 something cheaper to reach for. The Zero 3 W is a tougher one to call though, as the Zero range has always lived and died by its price, and I can’t imagine the BCM2711 being as cheap to build around as the RP3A0.

## Thoughts

On the whole, I like what I’m seeing here. The Zero 3 W looks like the upgrade a lot of people have been asking for since the Zero 2 W landed, and the 4 Model A feels like a sensible way of squeezing more life out of the Pi 4 platform at a time when components aren’t getting any cheaper. The external antenna support on the 4 Model A is a really nice touch if it makes it to the final board.

Saying that, everything above comes from device tree files rather than an official spec sheet, so mileage may vary when the real thing turns up. Kernel support landing ahead of launch is usually a good sign that it’s not far off, and you can bet I’ll be throwing both the Zero 3 W and the 4 Model A onto [sbc.compare](https://sbc.compare/) as soon as I can get one in my hands.

Which of the two are you more excited about? Do let me know in the comments!

**Sources**

**Related posts:**[Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W vs Zero W Benchmarks – Pi Zero Showdown](https://bret.dk/raspberry-pi-zero-2-w-benchmarks-comparison/) – [1GB Raspberry Pi 5 Launched Alongside Price Increases](https://bret.dk/1gb-raspberry-pi-5-launched-alongside-price-increases/)

##### [Bret](https://bret.dk/author/bret/ "Author Bret")

Bret has worked with Raspberry Pi computers for almost 10 years now and in that time he's benchmarked and tested over 30 Single Board computers. In his day job, he's a systems administrator for a large cloud computing provider.

Title: Police Are Using AI to Pull Over Drivers for ‘Suspicious’ Behavior

URL Source: https://gizmodo.com/police-are-using-ai-to-pull-over-drivers-for-suspicious-behavior-2000831220

Published Time: 2026-10-27T16:20:46+00:00

Markdown Content:
Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) aren’t just helping police investigate crimes anymore. They’re now being used to flag drivers for supposedly “suspicious” driving patterns.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) sounded the alarm Monday in a [blog post](https://www.aclu.org/news/privacy-technology/ai-driven-police-stops) on Monday, warning that law enforcement agencies across the United States are increasingly using license plate readers and AI-powered tools to pull over drivers even if they aren’t suspected of having committed a specific crime.

The post opens with the story of Grace Knowles, a woman in her 20s from northern Virginia who took a road trip through Oregon, Texas, and Louisiana in September 2025. On her way to Florida, she was pulled over by an officer who claimed she had spent too much time driving in the left lane.

The officer questioned Knowles about her travels and asked for proof that she had been in New Orleans. He eventually identified himself as a special agent with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) that was on a project for human and drug trafficking. He told her that her license plate had been flagged for suspicious travel patterns.

After she convinced him she was just on a road trip, he offered to show her what he was looking at on a computer in his car.

“It was basically a heat map of the U.S., and I could see different circles where I’d been, and when he clicked on it, it was a photo of my license plate,” Knowles told the ACLU.

When she asked how authorities had collected images of her license plate, the officer told her the cameras were everywhere, including on top of highway signs.

The ACLU warns that encounters like Knowles’ could become more common.

“For many people, those encounters will be far more fraught, frightening and dangerous than what Knowles experienced,” wrote Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst with the ACLU.

## ALPRs facing growing pushback nationwide

The warning comes as ALPRs are already facing growing backlash.

Companies like Flock Safety and Axon have become known in recent years for selling ALPR systems to law enforcement, which scan license plates as vehicles pass, collecting vehicle information along with the time and location they were spotted. Police can then search that data during investigations.

Privacy advocates, however, warn that the cameras collect location data on millions of people who are not suspected of crimes, often without a warrant, probable cause, or reasonable suspicion. There have also been reports of the systems leading to [mistakes](https://www.cbsnews.com/colorado/news/flock-cameras-lead-colorado-police-wrong-suspect/) and rampant [misuse](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/08/02/how-police-officers-used-vast-network-cameras-spy-their-exes/) by law enforcement.

An August YouGov survey found that [46% of respondents opposed](https://yougov.com/en-us/daily-results/20260824-a9b53-1) law enforcement using the technology in their communities, while 38% supported it.

Law enforcement agencies around the country, including the [Los Angeles Police Department](https://gizmodo.com/flock-says-we-hope-to-resume-work-with-lapd-after-getting-dropped-2000785092), have suspended or even ended their Flock contracts amid the growing backlash.

Knowles’ story is far from the only case raising concerns about how police are using license plate data.

In March, The Markup [reported](https://themarkup.org/privacy/2026/03/06/he-saw-an-abandoned-trailer-then-he-uncovered-a-surveillance-network-on-californias-border#:~:text=Pulling%20over) that a California grandmother was questioned by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CPB) officers about how often she visited local casinos. In [another case](https://www.404media.co/cops-used-flock-to-track-a-man-across-state-lines-to-create-pretext-to-search-his-car-for-weed/), a man was targeted for a traffic stop after repeatedly driving back and forth between Wisconsin and Michigan, which local police described as “a known source State for Marijuana.”

Earlier this month, a federal jury in Texas sided with a man who [sued](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/10/driver-wins-76-after-alpr-led-to-bogus-traffic-stop-drug-searches/) over what his attorneys described as an “unconstitutional traffic stop scheme” enabled by “AI-powered” license plate readers. According to the lawsuit, he was pulled over after his license plate was flagged for driving from Houston to Carrizo Springs, staying overnight, and returning home the following day.

Meanwhile, WIRED [reported](https://www.wired.com/story/flock-safety-os-investigate/) this month that Flock had developed an AI-powered investigative tool that “can identify drivers and track vehicles by their patterns of movement alone.”

Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Title: Tailscale SSH: Investigation and remediation update

URL Source: https://tailscale.com/ssh-investigation-update

Markdown Content:
**Published October 26th 2026.**

We're investigating security vulnerabilities affecting Tailscale SSH and wanted to share an update on what we've found, what we're doing about it, and what customers should know.

Our engineering and security teams have been investigating the reported issues with help from external security specialists. This builds on work already underway, which we've accelerated to address the findings and prepare fixes.

## [What we've found](https://tailscale.com/ssh-investigation-update#what-weve-found)

Most of the Tailscale SSH issues we've identified concern privilege escalation. In some circumstances, someone already authorized to connect over Tailscale SSH may be able to perform actions beyond the permissions of their configured local user, including potentially gaining elevated privileges.

These are serious security issues, and we're treating them accordingly.

Exploitation depends on the permissions granted to the connecting user or device, the system's configuration, and other conditions. We're continuing to verify the full scope of the findings and which configurations may be affected.

**Based on our current assessment, we're not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH.**

Our engineers have implemented fixes for most of the issues identified and are completing testing ahead of a patched client release.

**We're targeting a release by the end of Tuesday 27 October**, subject to successful completion of testing. We'll update this page when the patched version is available, or if that timeline changes.

We're continuing to review the remaining findings and verify that our changes address the underlying problems.

## [What customers can do now](https://tailscale.com/ssh-investigation-update#what-customers-can-do-now)

While we're preparing the update, we recommend reviewing your Tailscale SSH configuration:

*   **Review SSH access policies.** Make sure access is limited to the users and devices that need it.
*   **Disable SSH forwarding if you don't need it.** Set `TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1` in the `tailscaled` service environment and restart the service. This disables SSH forwarding without disabling Tailscale SSH entirely, and mitigates several of the more serious findings.
*   **Review access to sensitive systems.** Consider temporarily tightening your Tailscale SSH access policies while we investigate, so that only the specific users and devices that need access can connect.
*   **Prepare to update.** Apply the patched Tailscale client release when it becomes available.

## [What happens next](https://tailscale.com/ssh-investigation-update#what-happens-next)

Once the fixes are available, we'll publish a security advisory detailing the confirmed vulnerabilities, affected versions and configurations, their impact, and how to address them. We will link to that here when available.

We'll follow that with a technical blog post explaining the findings, the underlying causes, and the engineering changes we've made, again linked here when published.

If our assessment changes or we identify any additional steps customers need to take, we'll communicate those.

If you have questions about your particular environment, please contact [Tailscale Support](https://tailscale.com/contact/support#support-form).

Last weekend I watched four people desperately trying to get a laptop to connect to a screen. I was happily observing their efforts, with zero intent to join in.

But someone nudged me: can't _you_ have a look at it?

My reply: "Haha sorry no! My experience is that adding more people will not solve this problem any quicker".

I was of course -- indirectly -- referring to Brooks's Law:

> "Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later."

It was formulated by computer scientist Frederick P. Brooks Jr. in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month, based on his experience managing the IBM OS/360 project.

However I got to thinking. Does this still hold up in the age of AI agents and LLMs?

At first glance, you’d think no. The traditional bottlenecks -- onboarding time, endless stand-ups, and office politics -- disappear overnight. An AI agent is up to speed in milliseconds and doesn't demand a coffee break.

But when you look closer, and the law hasn't vanished. It just mutated.

The famous ["Baby Problem"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooks%27s_law#:~:text=Adding%20more%20people,in%20one%20month%22.) remains: nine agents still can’t deliver a baby in one month. Sequential tasks are still sequential.

Overhead hasn't disappeared; it shifted: instead of managing people, you are now managing agents. Someone still needs to define "done", review the code, catch hallucinations, and stitch the pieces together.

That someone is you.

Throw nine autonomous agents at a single codebase without crystal-clear orchestration, and they will happily rewrite each other's work in a high-speed loop.

Maybe the 2026 update to Brooks’s Law should be:

> "Adding agents to a project with unclear requirements gets you the wrong answer faster."
